q: Which statement best describes the T568B wiring standard?
options: The preferred wiring scheme for federal government installations
A wiring scheme identical in pinout to the T568A scheme
A wiring scheme used only for analog telephone lines
The common U.S. Ethernet wiring standard using the orange pair first
explain: T568B places the orange pair first and is the de facto standard in the U.S. T568A and T568B are both valid, but both ends of a cable must use the same scheme.

q: What is riser-rated (CMR) cable designed for?
options: Vertical runs between floors in a building
Horizontal runs under desks in an open office
Runs through plenum air-handling spaces above ceilings
Direct-burial outdoor runs between separate buildings
explain: Riser-rated (CMR) cable is designed for vertical runs between floors and helps prevent fire from spreading floor to floor. Plenum spaces require the stricter plenum-rated (CMP) cable.

q: What problem do dirty fiber-optic connectors most commonly cause?
options: Lower attenuation and more stable link performance
High insertion loss and intermittent, flapping links
Automatic cleaning of the fiber end face over time
Higher throughput because of increased light reflection
explain: Dirt on a fiber end face blocks and scatters light, causing high loss and intermittent links. Inspecting and cleaning connectors is the first step for most fiber faults.

q: Where should security cameras be placed for the best coverage?
options: Only in exterior parking lots and loading areas
At building entries and in sensitive areas such as server rooms
Only in break rooms and other low-risk common areas
Only on upper floors away from public access points
explain: Cameras should cover ingress and egress points and sensitive areas such as server rooms so incidents can be detected and reviewed. Placement should also respect privacy requirements.

q: What is a Yagi or dish antenna primarily used for?
options: Providing omnidirectional coverage to nearby wireless clients
Providing low-gain coverage inside a single room
Focusing a signal for a point-to-point wireless bridge
Receiving signals equally from all directions at once
explain: Yagi and dish antennas are high-gain directional antennas that focus a signal in one direction. They are commonly used for point-to-point bridges between buildings, not for serving local clients.

q: What happens if Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) settings do not match on both IPsec peers?
options: Phase 2 negotiates using the weaker peer's settings automatically
Phase 1 fails and no security association is formed at all
Traffic passes without encryption until the settings align
Phase 2 fails, so the settings must be aligned on both peers
explain: PFS Diffie-Hellman groups must match on both peers for Phase 2 (quick mode) to succeed. A mismatch breaks Phase 2 even if Phase 1 completed.

q: What is the purpose of hot/cold aisle containment in a data center?
options: To mix hot exhaust air and cold intake air in each aisle
To improve cooling efficiency by separating intake and exhaust air
To increase rack inlet temperatures to reduce humidity
To eliminate the need for any raised-floor cooling system
explain: Hot/cold aisle containment keeps cold intake air separate from hot exhaust air. This prevents mixing, improves cooling efficiency, and lowers cooling costs.

q: What should wireless monitoring track in addition to access point uptime?
options: Only whether each access point responds to a ping
Only the number of access points currently online
Interference, rogue access points, and client health
Only the wired switch ports connected to access points
explain: Wireless health is more than AP uptime. Monitoring should track interference, rogue APs, and client health such as signal, retries, and connection quality.

q: What is the purpose of a vendor field notice?
options: To warn customers about a known hardware defect or failure risk
To advertise a new product line and current promotions
To announce end-of-sale dates for unrelated software products
To provide routine pricing updates for support contracts
explain: A field notice warns customers about a known hardware defect or failure risk, often with a proactive replacement program. Acting on it prevents surprise failures in production.

q: Because encrypted traffic hides payload contents from monitoring tools, how should a team maintain visibility?
options: Block all encrypted traffic so it can be inspected in clear text
Rely only on full packet capture of every encrypted flow
Use metadata, flow data, and endpoint telemetry for visibility
Disable monitoring of encrypted traffic and focus only on clear text
explain: When payloads are opaque, metadata such as flow records and TLS fingerprints (for example JA3) plus endpoint telemetry from EDR still provide visibility. This fills the gap without breaking encryption.

q: What does S/MIME do?
options: Encrypts web traffic between a browser and a web server
Signs and encrypts email using digital certificates
Encrypts email using a web-of-trust model without certificates
Signs and encrypts files stored on a web server
explain: S/MIME uses PKI digital certificates to sign and encrypt email. This differs from PGP, which historically uses a web-of-trust model instead of a central PKI.

q: What does sandboxing an email attachment do?
options: Detonates the file safely in isolation before it is delivered
Compresses the file to reduce mailbox storage usage
Deletes the email automatically without analyzing the file
Converts the file to a different format for the recipient
explain: Sandboxing opens (detonates) an attachment in an isolated environment and watches its behavior before delivery. This can catch malicious documents that static filters miss.

q: What is Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) used for?
options: Routing broadcast traffic between IP subnets
Routing multicast traffic between network segments
Routing unicast traffic between autonomous systems
Resolving domain names to IP addresses for multicast groups
explain: PIM is a multicast routing protocol that routes multicast traffic across routers between segments. It works independently of the unicast routing protocol in use.

q: 802.1X authentication is failing because of clock skew on client devices. What should you do first?
options: Synchronize client clocks using NTP
Replace the clients' digital certificates
Disable certificate validation on the clients
Increase the 802.1X reauthentication timer
explain: Certificate validation fails when a device clock is far from the correct time, which breaks 802.1X. Synchronizing devices with NTP fixes the skew and should be done before replacing certificates.

q: What does a DNS NS record identify?
options: The authoritative name servers for a DNS zone
The email servers that accept mail for a domain
The web servers that host a domain's website
The client devices that query a DNS zone
explain: An NS record delegates a zone to its authoritative name servers. Mail servers are identified by MX records and web hosts are typically reached through A, AAAA, or CNAME records.

q: A PoE-powered device will not power on. Which causes should you check first?
options: An exceeded PoE budget, a faulty cable, or a non-PoE switch port
A VLAN mismatch, a DNS failure, or a duplicate IP address
A spanning-tree block, a routing loop, or a QoS misconfiguration
An expired certificate, an NTP failure, or a firewall rule
explain: Power problems are checked at the power layer first: whether the switch PoE budget is exceeded, whether the cable and pairs are good, and whether the port is actually a PoE port that can classify the device.

q: Which set lists Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) port states?
options: Open, closed, filtered, and established
Up, down, testing, and disabled
Blocking, listening, learning, and forwarding
Active, standby, backup, and forwarding
explain: Classic STP ports move through blocking, listening, and learning before reaching forwarding. A port only forwards once STP has confirmed the path is loop-free.

q: What is the purpose of a privacy screen on a monitor?
options: To prevent shoulder surfing by limiting the viewing angle
To prevent glare from overhead office lighting
To protect the monitor from physical damage during travel
To filter blue light to reduce eye strain for the user
explain: A privacy filter narrows the viewing angle so people beside the user cannot read the screen. This protects sensitive data from shoulder surfing in open offices and while traveling.

q: What does STP Root Guard do?
options: Blocks superior BPDUs on a designated port to protect the root bridge placement
Blocks all BPDUs on an access port connected to an end device
Disables STP on a port to allow a faster convergence time
Forces a port to become the new root port for the topology
explain: Root Guard is applied on designated ports and blocks superior BPDUs that would try to make another switch the root. This preserves the intended root bridge placement.

q: Why must log timestamps be synchronized with NTP across devices?
options: So events from different devices can be correlated accurately
So log files use less storage space on each device
So devices can forward logs without a syslog server
So log rotation occurs at the same time on every device
explain: If device clocks differ, events cannot be lined up in time order across devices. NTP-synchronized timestamps make multi-device correlation and incident timelines possible.

q: What is a jump host?
options: A router that provides the default gateway for admin subnets
A hardened server used as the entry point for administrative access
A user workstation that administrators share for daily tasks
A backup server that stores copies of administrative credentials
explain: A jump host is a hardened, monitored server that administrators connect to first (with MFA and logging) before reaching target systems. It limits direct administrative exposure of those targets.

q: What does a reflexive ACL do?
options: Applies a static rule set that never changes after it is configured
Filters IPv6 traffic using only the source address of each packet
Dynamically allows return traffic for sessions initiated from inside
Inspects encrypted traffic and decrypts it before forwarding it onward
explain: A reflexive ACL creates temporary, dynamic entries to allow return traffic for sessions started from inside. This avoids writing broad permanent permits for inbound traffic.

q: What is the role of a wireless LAN controller?
options: To act as a single access point for a small office network
To route traffic between different IP subnets and VLANs
To centrally manage access points, configurations, and roaming
To provide Power over Ethernet to all connected access points
explain: A wireless controller centrally manages many APs, pushing configurations and policies and coordinating roaming. The APs themselves still provide the radio coverage.

q: How is traffic for the native VLAN carried on an 802.1Q trunk?
options: It is carried with a special encrypted VLAN tag
It is carried untagged across the trunk link
It is always carried as VLAN 1, regardless of configuration
It is dropped unless the trunk is configured as an access port
explain: Traffic for the native VLAN is sent untagged on an 802.1Q trunk by default. If the native VLAN does not match on both ends, connectivity breaks and VLAN hopping risk increases.

q: What should happen to action items identified in a postmortem?
options: They should be documented but left unassigned for the team
They should be reviewed only if the same incident recurs
They should be assigned informally without a completion date
They should be assigned an owner and tracked to completion
explain: Postmortem action items need an owner and tracking to completion, otherwise the same failure recurs. A postmortem without follow-through does not improve reliability.

q: Users across the entire site report that everything is slow. Where should you investigate first?
options: A single user's workstation and its local network cable
The DNS settings on one affected user's computer only
The wireless settings on a single access point in one room
The core and distribution layers and the upstream provider link
explain: When slowness affects everyone, the cause is usually in shared infrastructure or the provider link, not one endpoint. Start at the core, distribution layer, and upstream connection.

q: Why would an organization record privileged administrator sessions?
options: To monitor the daily productivity of individual administrators
To replace the need for multifactor authentication for admins
To capture privileged actions for accountability and forensic review
To provide training videos for new members of the support team
explain: Recording sessions through a jump host captures what privileged users actually did. The recordings support accountability and provide evidence during forensic investigations.

q: What is a change freeze period?
options: A period when emergency changes are processed without any approval
A period when changes are halted during critical business times
A period when all network devices are powered down for maintenance
A period when users are prevented from submitting any new tickets
explain: A freeze period halts non-emergency changes during critical business times, such as retail holidays or financial quarter-close. This reduces the risk of an outage when the business can least afford one.

q: Why would you send syslog messages over TLS?
options: To protect the confidentiality of log data while it is in transit
To send logs using the default unencrypted UDP transport method
To reduce the size of log messages before they are transmitted
To guarantee that the syslog server never needs authentication
explain: Logs often contain sensitive addresses, usernames, and errors, so encrypting syslog in transit with TLS protects its confidentiality. Traditional syslog over UDP sends that data in clear text.

q: What does a KVM-over-IP device allow an administrator to do?
options: Remotely control a server at the hardware level, even if its OS has crashed
Remotely control a server only after its operating system has fully booted
Remotely monitor a server's power usage without controlling its console
Remotely update a server's firmware without accessing its management console
explain: KVM-over-IP provides remote keyboard, video, and mouse control at the hardware level, so it works even when the operating system has crashed. Because of that power, it must be secured like a jump host.

q: What does a data diode do?
options: Allows data to flow in both directions through a hardware filter
Acts as a stateful firewall between two security zones
Encrypts data in both directions between two networks
Enforces one-way data flow at the hardware level
explain: A data diode is hardware that physically allows data to flow in only one direction. It is used for high-security transfers where any return path must be impossible.

q: What is the purpose of a guest VLAN?
options: To provide trusted staff with access to internal servers
To provide visitors with unrestricted access to the LAN
To isolate visitor traffic and allow internet-only access
To provide a backup VLAN if the corporate VLAN fails
explain: A guest VLAN quarantines visitor traffic away from internal resources, typically allowing internet access only, often with client isolation. Guests should not be able to reach the corporate LAN.

q: What is a storage area network (SAN)?
options: A wireless network that connects storage devices to clients
A local area network that provides file sharing to all users
A dedicated high-speed fabric that provides block-level storage access
A wide area network that replicates files between office sites
explain: A SAN is a dedicated high-speed storage fabric, such as Fibre Channel or iSCSI, that gives servers block-level access to storage. It is separate from a general-purpose LAN or WAN.

q: What should metrics dashboards for organizational leadership primarily show?
options: Long-term trends in uptime, response time, and capacity
Real-time packet captures from every network segment
Detailed device configurations for each network switch
Individual ticket assignments for each support engineer
explain: Leadership dashboards should show trends, not just current outages — for example uptime trends, mean time to repair, and capacity forecasts. Those trends inform investment decisions.

q: What does a time-based ACL do?
options: Applies access rules only during specified time periods or schedules
Applies the same access rules continuously, regardless of the time
Changes a user's password automatically after a set time period
Logs access attempts and reports them at scheduled intervals only
explain: A time-based ACL enforces its rules only on a defined schedule, such as business hours. It is commonly used to limit guest or contractor access to approved times.

q: When should a technician stop troubleshooting an issue and escalate it?
options: As soon as the first troubleshooting step does not resolve it
Only after working on the issue continuously for several days
Only when the affected user requests that it be escalated
When the assigned time box expires or the risk of impact grows
explain: Escalation should occur when the predefined time box expires or when risk or impact grows beyond the technician's scope. Escalating on defined triggers is good practice, not failure.

q: What is a break-glass account?
options: An emergency access account that triggers alerting when it is used
A shared account that all administrators use for daily work
A standard account that is exempt from multifactor authentication
A backup account that automatically replaces a locked-out account
explain: A break-glass account provides sealed emergency access for lockout situations, with strong alerting whenever it is used. Its use should be rare, audited, and investigated.

q: What do late collisions on an Ethernet link most commonly indicate?
options: Interference from a nearby high-voltage power source
A duplex mismatch between the two ends of the link
A VLAN mismatch between the two connected switches
A spanning-tree loop on the connected switch ports
explain: Late collisions occur after the first 64 bytes of a frame and most commonly indicate a duplex mismatch, where one side is half-duplex and the other is full-duplex. Both ends must be set consistently.

q: Why would you administratively shut down a flapping interface during an incident?
options: To stabilize the network while you investigate the cause
To permanently remove the device connected to that interface
To force the connected device to obtain a new IP address
To test whether users notice the loss of that connection
explain: Shutting a flapping interface stops the repeated up/down churn from destabilizing routing and spanning tree. You can then investigate the cause while the rest of the network stays stable.

q: What does avoiding tunnel vision mean during troubleshooting?
options: Spending more time on the first theory until it is proven
Re-validating your assumptions and rechecking the basics
Asking another technician to take over every difficult ticket
Documenting each step before testing any possible cause
explain: Avoiding tunnel vision means stepping back, re-validating assumptions, and rechecking basics such as Layer 1 when you are stuck. The first theory is often the thing blocking progress.

q: What is the primary purpose of a ticketing system?
options: To provide users with a self-service portal for password resets
To track work, incidents, and changes and provide an audit trail
To monitor network devices and alert on performance thresholds
To store network configurations and back them up automatically
explain: A ticketing system tracks incidents, requests, and changes from opening to resolution. That record becomes the audit trail for what was done and why.

q: What does an escalation matrix define?
options: The order in which network changes must be approved
The list of all users who may submit a support ticket
The schedule for routine maintenance and patching windows
Which responders should handle incidents at each severity level
explain: An escalation matrix maps incident severity to the responders who should be engaged, so a high-severity (P1) incident reaches senior responders immediately instead of waiting in a queue.

q: What does airtime fairness do on a wireless network?
options: Prevents slow clients from monopolizing the wireless medium
Gives the fastest clients all of the available airtime first
Disables slower wireless standards to improve overall speed
Assigns each client an equal share of total throughput only
explain: Airtime fairness gives clients a fair share of airtime rather than letting a slow client hold the medium while sending at a low rate. This keeps the WLAN responsive for faster clients.

q: Why is adjacent-channel interference more harmful than co-channel interference?
options: Adjacent channels use a weaker signal than co-channel networks
Adjacent channels are unplanned and therefore use more power
Co-channel networks transmit on completely different frequencies
Radios on overlapping channels cannot coordinate their transmissions
explain: Radios on the same (co-channel) channel can hear each other and coordinate access, but radios on partially overlapping adjacent channels cannot, so they corrupt each other's frames. Use only non-overlapping channels.

q: Which mechanisms are used to detect errors in transmitted data?
options: Encryption and user authentication
Retransmission and flow control only
Checksums and cyclic redundancy checks (CRCs)
Compression and packet fragmentation
explain: Error detection uses checksums and CRCs, such as the frame check sequence, to catch corruption. Retransmission (ARQ) can then recover a damaged frame, but it does not by itself detect the error.

q: What speed and distance does Cat5e cable support for Ethernet?
options: 100 Mbps up to 100 meters
1 Gbps up to 100 meters
10 Gbps up to 100 meters
10 Mbps up to 100 meters
explain: Cat5e supports Gigabit Ethernet (1 Gbps) up to 100 meters. For comparison, Cat6 supports 10 Gbps to about 55 meters and Cat6a supports 10 Gbps to 100 meters.

q: What does global server load balancing (GSLB) do?
options: Directs users to the most suitable data center for their request
Balances traffic only between servers in a single data center
Resolves domain names without considering server health or location
Distributes traffic only by using round-robin DNS records alone
explain: GSLB steers users across sites to the best data center, using DNS together with health checks, proximity, and capacity. This differs from local load balancing, which works within one site.

q: What does zero-touch provisioning do?
options: Requires an engineer on site to configure each new device manually
Configures a device only after a user submits a support ticket
Provides a device with an IP address but no configuration file
Automatically configures a new device when it is first connected
explain: Zero-touch provisioning automatically bootstraps and configures a new device when it connects, often using DHCP options to reach a provisioning server. Branches can be deployed without an engineer on site.

q: How many bits are in an IPv4 address, and how is it written?
options: 128 bits, written as eight hexadecimal groups
16 bits, written as two decimal octets
32 bits, written as four decimal octets
48 bits, written as six hexadecimal octets
explain: An IPv4 address is 32 bits long and written as four decimal octets, such as 192.168.1.1. A 128-bit address written in hexadecimal groups is IPv6, and a 48-bit address is a MAC address.

q: How should health check intervals for load-balanced servers be chosen?
options: To balance fast failure detection against the load checks place on servers
To run as frequently as possible regardless of the load on servers
To run at a single fixed interval for every application and server
To check servers only when users report that an application is down
explain: Shorter health check intervals detect failures faster but add load to servers and load balancers. The interval should balance detection speed against that overhead.

q: What is an implicit deny in an access control list (ACL)?
options: A rule at the end of the ACL that blocks any traffic not explicitly permitted
An explicit rule an administrator adds to permit all remaining traffic
A rule that logs permitted traffic without blocking any traffic at all
A rule that allows traffic that matches no other rule in the ACL
explain: Every ACL ends with an implicit deny that blocks any traffic not explicitly permitted above it. Administrators add explicit permit rules above that final deny.

q: How can an organization prevent tailgating into a secure area?
options: By using badge readers, mantraps, and security awareness training
By using wider entrance doors and longer badge reader timeouts
By allowing visitors to enter if they are following an employee
By relying only on security cameras to record every entrance
explain: Tailgating is prevented with badge-controlled entry, mantraps that allow one person at a time, and awareness training so staff challenge strangers and escort visitors. Cameras alone only record the event.

q: What happens when a copper cable is sharply kinked?
options: Its resistance decreases and signal speed increases noticeably
Its connectors loosen but its electrical properties stay the same
Its shielding improves and crosstalk between pairs is reduced
Its impedance changes, causing signal reflections and return loss
explain: A kink changes the cable's impedance at that point, which causes reflections and return loss that degrade the signal. Damaged sections should be replaced rather than straightened and reused.

q: What is the purpose of a public status page during an incident?
options: To communicate outage status and updates to customers publicly
To advertise new services to customers during the outage period
To collect diagnostic logs from customers affected by an outage
To redirect customers to a backup data center automatically
explain: A public status page communicates outage status and progress updates to customers in one place. Regular, honest updates build trust and reduce duplicate support contacts.

q: What is the purpose of contact lists and runbook documentation?
options: To store the passwords that on-call responders need for devices
To record the configuration history of every network device
To list the vendors and contract terms for all network services
To guide on-call responders through incidents and escalation paths
explain: Runbooks and contact lists guide on-call responders step by step, including escalation paths and who to contact. Good runbooks cut mean time to repair during an incident.

q: What does a syslog collector do?
options: Centralizes logs from many devices for analysis and retention
Filters traffic between networks based on a set of rules
Deletes old logs from devices to free up local storage space
Generates test log messages to verify that logging is working
explain: A syslog collector centralizes logs sent from many devices into one place. Central collection enables correlation, searching, and retention that individual devices cannot provide.

q: How are rogue DHCP servers blocked on a switched network?
options: By enabling DHCP snooping and trusting only designated uplink ports for DHCP offers
By assigning static IP addresses to every client on the network
By enabling port security to limit the number of MAC addresses per port
By filtering DHCP traffic at the network's perimeter firewall only
explain: DHCP snooping builds a binding table and only allows DHCP server messages (offers) on trusted ports, typically uplinks to legitimate servers. Offers arriving on untrusted access ports from a rogue server are dropped.

q: What happens if an access port is assigned to the wrong VLAN?
options: The device is placed on a trunk and can reach all VLANs
The device is logically isolated from the resources in its intended VLAN
The device automatically moves itself to the correct VLAN
The device receives a faster connection through the new VLAN
explain: An access port in the wrong VLAN places the device in the wrong broadcast domain, logically isolating it from its intended servers and gateway. Verify the port's access VLAN against the plan.

q: What must you do to verify that a fix has resolved a problem?
options: Close the ticket and record the time the fix was applied
Ask the user to monitor the system and report any recurrence
Retest using the original symptoms and failure scenario
Restart the affected device and confirm that it boots correctly
explain: Verification means retesting the original symptoms in the original failure scenario to confirm they no longer occur. Closing the ticket or rebooting the device alone does not prove the fix worked.

q: Why would you rate-limit a noisy host during an investigation?
options: To permanently disconnect the host from the network
To contain its impact while you investigate its behavior
To force the host to request a new address from DHCP
To improve the host's performance by reducing its traffic
explain: Rate-limiting (policing) a noisy host contains its impact on others while you investigate, without fully disconnecting it. This buys time to identify the cause.

q: What does a service mesh do in a microservices environment?
options: Provides physical switching between containers on a host
Routes traffic between branch offices across a wide area network
Filters traffic between services using a perimeter firewall appliance
Manages service-to-service communication, including discovery, TLS, and policy
explain: A service mesh manages communication between microservices, typically through sidecar proxies that handle service discovery, mutual TLS, and policy. It operates between services, not at the WAN or perimeter.

q: What is the purpose of a password vault for privileged credentials?
options: To centralize secrets and provide auditing, rotation, and controlled access
To store secrets in a spreadsheet shared by the administration team
To allow administrators to share one password across all systems
To replace multifactor authentication for privileged user accounts
explain: A password vault centralizes privileged secrets with controlled checkout, auditing, and automatic rotation. This is far safer than shared spreadsheets or reused passwords.

q: What is an emergency change?
options: A change that fixes a critical issue quickly, with approval documented retroactively
A routine change that follows the standard approval process and schedule
A change that is made without any record or follow-up review at all
A change that must wait for the next scheduled maintenance window
explain: An emergency change fixes a critical issue quickly to restore service, with approval and documentation completed retroactively. Speed is balanced with accountability, not with skipping records entirely.

q: An LTE backup link fails to register on the cellular network. What should you check?
options: The link's Ethernet speed, duplex, and VLAN assignment
The link's DNS, DHCP, and default gateway configuration
The APN settings, cellular signal, and account status
The link's routing table, NAT rules, and firewall policies
explain: Cellular registration failures are usually caused by an incorrect APN, weak signal, or an inactive account or data plan. Check those cellular-specific items before changing LAN settings.

q: What information does capacity planning use?
options: Vendor specifications for the maximum capacity of each device
Estimates provided by users about their future bandwidth needs
Historical growth trends to forecast when upgrades will be needed
Current utilization measured at a single point in time only
explain: Capacity planning analyzes historical utilization and growth trends to forecast when links or devices will saturate. That forecast drives timely upgrades before performance suffers.

q: What does threshold-based alerting do?
options: Fires an alert when a monitored metric crosses a defined limit
Fires an alert only when a user manually reports a problem
Fires an alert at a fixed time each day regardless of metrics
Fires an alert only after a device has completely failed
explain: Threshold alerting fires when a metric crosses a defined limit, such as 80% bandwidth utilization or a rising error count. Sane thresholds catch problems early, before a full outage.

q: Why should you monitor Power over Ethernet (PoE) power draw on a switch?
options: To verify that each connected device is using the correct VLAN
To prevent the total draw from exceeding the switch's PoE budget
To measure the data throughput of each powered device over time
To confirm that each device has negotiated the correct duplex mode
explain: Each switch has a total PoE power budget. Monitoring draw as powered devices are added prevents overruns that would stop new devices from powering on.

q: You observe packet loss but no link congestion. What should you check first?
options: The Quality of Service policies applied to the affected traffic
The routing table and default gateway on the affected devices
The DNS configuration on the clients experiencing the loss
The physical layer for cable, optic, error, and duplex problems
explain: Packet loss with clean, uncongested queues usually points to the physical layer — a bad cable or optic, interface errors, or a duplex problem. Check counters and Layer 1 before changing QoS or routing.

q: A client has been assigned an address in the 169.254.x.x range. What does this indicate?
options: The client was configured with a static address in that range
The client failed to obtain an address from DHCP and used APIPA
The client connected through a VPN that uses that address range
The client obtained a valid address from a rogue DHCP server
explain: An address in 169.254.0.0/16 is an APIPA link-local address a Windows client self-assigns when DHCP fails. Check the DHCP server, scope, relay, and Layer 2 path to the client.

q: What is the purpose of preventive measures after an incident is resolved?
options: To document the incident for the next scheduled audit review
To assign responsibility for the incident to a specific team
To reduce the cost of the response by closing the ticket sooner
To stop the problem from recurring, using monitoring or redundancy
explain: Preventive measures stop the same problem from recurring — for example adding the missing alert, a spare, redundancy, or a diverse path. Resolving the immediate incident alone leaves the root risk in place.

q: Why would you perform an SNMP walk during a network fault?
options: To change device configurations quickly without using the CLI
To test whether a device responds to ICMP echo requests
To capture packets flowing through the affected device's ports
To quickly retrieve counters and status information from a device
explain: An SNMP walk quickly retrieves interface counters and status, such as the ifTable, including errors, discards, and utilization. That data helps locate a fault without logging in to every device.

q: What does intent verification do in a network automation system?
options: Compares the initial configuration of a device to its factory defaults
Continuously checks that the actual network state matches the intended state
Verifies that an application meets its functional requirements before release
Requires an engineer to manually approve every automated configuration change
explain: Intent verification continuously compares the actual state of the network with the intended state and flags or corrects drift. This closed loop keeps an automated network in compliance with its design.

q: What does a site-to-site VPN do?
options: Connects entire networks to each other securely over the internet
Connects a single remote user to a corporate network over the internet
Connects two devices on the same local network without encryption
Connects a branch office using a dedicated leased line only
explain: A site-to-site VPN, typically IPsec, connects whole networks — such as branch LANs — to each other securely across the public internet. A single-user connection is a remote-access VPN instead.

q: What does a network tap do?
options: Passively copies traffic on a link so it can be monitored or captured
Actively inspects traffic and blocks any traffic that matches a rule
Routes traffic between two networks based on its destination address
Forwards traffic to a different port based on its VLAN assignment
explain: A network tap passively copies traffic on a link and sends the copy to monitoring or capture tools, such as an IDS. It does not sit inline or affect the live traffic.

q: Which set contains only non-overlapping channels in the 2.4 GHz band (U.S.)?
options: Channels 5, 6, and 7
Channels 1, 2, and 3
Channels 2, 6, and 10
Channels 1, 6, and 11
explain: In the 2.4 GHz band in the U.S., only channels 1, 6, and 11 do not overlap each other. Access points should be planned on these channels to avoid adjacent-channel interference.

q: What does immutable storage do for backup data?
options: Stores data at a slower speed to reduce the cost of backup storage
Prevents backup data from being deleted or modified for a set period
Stores data only in an archive tier that is rarely accessed by users
Encrypts backup data so that only authorized users can read it
explain: Immutable storage, such as WORM or object-lock, prevents data from being deleted or modified until a retention period expires. This protects backups from attacker or ransomware deletion.

q: What does a TCP zero window indicate?
options: The receiving host cannot accept more data at this time
The sending host has no more data left to transmit
The sender's congestion window has grown too large
The receiving host is ready for data at the maximum rate
explain: A TCP zero window means the receiver's buffer is full and it is advertising that it cannot accept more data, so the sender pauses. Check the receiving host's resources and application.

q: What do the first 24 bits of a MAC address identify?
options: The individual user assigned to the network interface card
The network segment on which the interface is currently located
The specific model and type of device using the address
The manufacturer, identified by the Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI)
explain: The first 24 bits of a MAC address are the Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI), assigned by the IEEE to the manufacturer. The remaining 24 bits identify the individual interface.

q: Why should multicast traffic be monitored?
options: To verify that unicast routing tables are converging correctly
To verify group joins, PIM state, and the health of multicast streams
To measure the throughput of unicast video streams on the network
To confirm that broadcast traffic is being forwarded between VLANs
explain: Multicast monitoring verifies that receivers are joining groups (IGMP), that PIM state is correct, and that streams such as IPTV remain continuous. Without it, multicast failures are hard to see.

q: Which service uses TCP port 445?
options: Network File System (NFS) file sharing
File Transfer Protocol (FTP) file transfer
Server Message Block (SMB) file sharing
Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) web traffic
explain: TCP port 445 is used by SMB for file sharing, in its modern direct-hosted form without NetBIOS. NFS, FTP, and HTTP use different ports.

q: Why are configuration differences (diffs) between versions useful?
options: They prove that a device was compliant at the time of an audit
They list every command that is available on a network device
They summarize the current configuration in a shorter report format
They reveal exactly what changed between two configuration versions
explain: A config diff compares an archived configuration, such as running versus last-known-good, and reveals exactly what changed. That makes it fast to spot the change that caused a problem.

q: What does Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) do?
options: Assigns IP addresses to clients and records their MAC addresses
Inspects DNS queries and blocks queries for malicious domains
Validates ARP messages against the DHCP snooping binding table
Encrypts ARP messages so they cannot be spoofed on the network
explain: DAI validates ARP messages against the DHCP snooping binding table and drops spoofed ARP. This is a key defense against man-in-the-middle attacks on the LAN.

q: How many usable host addresses does an IPv4 /24 prefix provide?
options: 254 usable host addresses
24 usable host addresses
510 usable host addresses
256 usable host addresses
explain: A /24 has 8 host bits, giving 2^8 = 256 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses, for 254 usable hosts. A /23 would provide 510 usable hosts.

q: Which service uses UDP ports 67 and 68?
options: Domain Name System (DNS) name resolution
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) address assignment
Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) file transfer
Network Time Protocol (NTP) time synchronization
explain: DHCP uses UDP port 67 on the server and UDP port 68 on the client. DNS uses port 53, TFTP uses port 69, and NTP uses port 123.

q: Why is prefix filtering applied to BGP advertisements?
options: To reduce the speed at which BGP updates are propagated
To block bogus, private, or reserved prefix announcements
To allow a router to accept every prefix it receives from peers
To convert prefixes received from one autonomous system to another
explain: BGP prefix filtering blocks bogus announcements, such as private or reserved prefixes leaking to the internet, and works with max-prefix limits. This protects routing integrity between peers.

q: What does firmware lifecycle management involve?
options: Tracking deployed firmware versions and vendor end-of-life dates
Installing the newest firmware on every device as soon as it releases
Keeping a manual list of devices without tracking their versions
Preventing any firmware updates until a device reaches end of life
explain: Firmware lifecycle management tracks which versions are deployed and when vendors end support for them. Knowing this prevents devices from running unsupported, vulnerable firmware unnoticed.

q: During troubleshooting, why is a faulty patch cord a common first item to swap out?
options: Because patch cords are designed only for use with fiber links
Because patch cords rarely fail compared with other components
Because patch cords cannot be tested with a standard cable tester
Because patch cords are frequently damaged and are easy to substitute with a spare
explain: Patch cords take frequent handling and bending and fail often, and swapping one for a known-good spare is fast and cheap. Always keep spares available for substitution testing.

q: Which service uses TCP port 443?
options: HTTPS, for TLS-encrypted web traffic
HTTP, for unencrypted web traffic
FTP, for unencrypted file transfer
Telnet, for unencrypted remote terminal access
explain: TCP port 443 carries HTTPS, web traffic encrypted with TLS. Unencrypted HTTP uses port 80, FTP uses ports 20/21, and Telnet uses port 23.

q: Only one user is experiencing slow performance while others on the same network are fine. What should you check first?
options: The user's cable, network adapter, and switch port
The organization's DNS servers and their configuration
The internet service provider's upstream connection
The core switch and its routing configuration
explain: When only one user is affected, isolate the problem at that user's edge first — cable, NIC, and switch port. Shared infrastructure such as the core or ISP would affect many users.

q: How does a mesh access point connect to the wireless network?
options: By using a wired Ethernet backhaul to the nearest switch
By acting as a router for all other access points in the mesh
By using a wireless backhaul to connect to other access points
By connecting directly to the wireless LAN controller by cable
explain: A mesh AP backhauls its traffic wirelessly through other APs instead of using a cable run. Mesh extends coverage to areas where Ethernet cabling is impractical.

q: What network conditions does voice traffic typically require to remain intelligible?
options: Best-effort delivery with no prioritization over other traffic
High bandwidth with no limits on latency or jitter variation
Low bandwidth with tolerance for delays of several seconds
One-way latency under 150 ms with minimal jitter
explain: Voice needs low delay and jitter, with a commonly used one-way latency budget of under 150 ms, rather than high bandwidth. Voice traffic should be prioritized with QoS and provisioned accordingly.

q: How does Cisco Smart Licensing manage software entitlements?
options: By storing a separate license file manually on each individual device
By providing all entitlements free of charge without any registration
By tying each entitlement permanently to a single device's serial number
By pooling entitlements centrally in the cloud for the organization
explain: Cisco Smart Licensing pools an organization's entitlements centrally in the cloud (Smart Account) rather than tying a file to each device. This simplifies moves, true-ups, and compliance checks.

q: What is a protocol in networking?
options: A physical device that connects two or more networks together
An address that identifies a device on an IP network uniquely
A formal set of rules that governs how devices communicate
A cable standard that defines how connectors are wired together
explain: A protocol is a formal set of rules that defines the format, order, and error handling of communication between devices. Devices, addresses, and cables are separate concepts.

q: What is a butt set used to test?
options: Analog telephone lines, by connecting at a terminal or demarc
Fiber-optic lines, by measuring light loss at each connector
Ethernet lines, by certifying cable speed and wire mapping
Coaxial lines, by measuring signal strength and interference
explain: A butt set is a lineman's handset used to test analog telephone (POTS) and DSL lines by clipping on at a terminal. It does not test fiber, Ethernet, or coax media.

q: How should an organization communicate during a major outage?
options: By keeping all outage information internal until service is restored
By waiting until the outage ends before providing any information
By relying on informal reports from users about the outage status
By providing regular, factual updates to stakeholders throughout the outage
explain: During an outage, communicate on a regular cadence with factual updates, even if the update is that work is still in progress. This keeps stakeholders calm and informed and reduces rumor.

q: What does Network Address Translation (NAT) translate?
options: Private IP addresses to public IP addresses
IPv4 addresses to IPv6 addresses for a dual-stack host
Hostnames to IP addresses for name resolution queries
MAC addresses to IP addresses for local delivery
explain: NAT translates private IP addresses to public IP addresses (and back), allowing many private hosts to share a smaller number of public addresses. Hostname-to-IP translation is DNS, and MAC-to-IP resolution involves ARP.

q: How should a screened subnet (DMZ) be designed for IPv6?
options: It is not needed because IPv6 addresses are not routable publicly
It should be built only for IPv4 because IPv6 cannot be segmented
It should apply the same DMZ segmentation principles used for IPv4
It should place all IPv6 hosts directly on the internal network
explain: IPv6 does not change network architecture principles: a screened subnet for IPv6 applies the same DMZ segmentation used for IPv4. Public-facing services still belong in a segmented zone, not on the internal network.

q: What is the purpose of a lessons-learned review after a major incident?
options: To determine which individual was responsible for causing the incident
To document the incident timeline without changing any processes
To improve processes and prevent similar incidents in the future
To produce a formal report that is filed for audit purposes
explain: A lessons-learned (post-incident) review turns an outage into systemic improvements to processes and systems. Its goal is prevention, not assigning blame to an individual.

q: What are IETF standards documents called?
options: IEEE standards specifications
International laws and regulations
ISO standards documents
Requests for Comments (RFCs)
explain: Standards from the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) are published as Requests for Comments (RFCs). RFCs define the core TCP/IP protocols and many internet standards.

q: Why are a jump server's logs especially valuable after a security incident?
options: They record the daily activity of standard end users on the network
They provide prime forensic evidence of privileged administrative access
They replace the logs kept on each individual target server entirely
They contain the passwords used during each administrative session
explain: Because administrative access is centralized through the jump server, its logs form a clean audit trail of privileged actions. That makes them prime forensic evidence after an incident.

q: What is the purpose of a floating static route?
options: To summarize multiple networks into a single advertised route
To load-balance traffic equally across two active links
To provide a backup route with a higher administrative distance
To replace dynamic routing with a permanent primary route
explain: A floating static route has a higher administrative distance than the primary route, so it stays unused until the primary route disappears, then it becomes active as a backup.

q: How does segmented network monitoring differ from perimeter-only monitoring?
options: It uses a single sensor placed at the Internet edge only
It places sensors in each network zone to watch internal traffic
It monitors only WAN links between branch offices
It replaces all internal sensors with cloud-based collectors
explain: Segmented monitoring places sensors inside each zone or segment, so lateral movement and internal threats are visible instead of only traffic crossing the perimeter.

q: What is the primary function of a console server (terminal server)?
options: To provide serial console access to many network devices
To provide wireless access to clients in an office
To provide Power over Ethernet to connected devices
To provide routing between different IP subnets
explain: A console server provides out-of-band serial access to the console ports of routers, switches, and other devices, so administrators can manage them even when the production network is down.

q: When is a compensating control most appropriate?
options: When a vulnerability can be patched immediately with no risk
When a control is added to increase performance of a system
When a system cannot be patched and the risk must be mitigated another way
When an organization wants to permanently replace all patching
explain: A compensating control reduces risk when the preferred fix, such as patching a legacy system, is not possible — for example by isolating the system and monitoring it closely.

q: What does Proxy ARP allow a router to do?
options: Answer ARP requests on behalf of hosts on other networks
Speed up ARP by caching entries for a longer period
Encrypt ARP traffic between hosts on the same subnet
Replace DNS for resolving hostnames to IP addresses
explain: With Proxy ARP, a router replies to an ARP request with its own MAC address for a destination on another network, so the sending host forwards the traffic to the router. It can mask subnetting errors and is usually disabled.

q: Under what condition does IP fragmentation occur?
options: When a packet is smaller than the link's MTU
When a packet's TTL expires in transit
When a destination host is unreachable
When a packet is larger than the MTU of a link it must cross
explain: Fragmentation occurs when a packet exceeds the maximum transmission unit (MTU) of a link. The packet is split into fragments that are reassembled at the final destination.

q: What is the role of a DHCP relay agent (IP helper)?
options: To act as a DHCP server and assign addresses itself
To assign static IP addresses to servers and printers
To block DHCP broadcast traffic from leaving a subnet
To forward DHCP broadcast requests across subnets to a server
explain: DHCP broadcasts do not cross routers, so a relay agent forwards client broadcasts as unicast to a DHCP server on another subnet, allowing one server to serve many VLANs.

q: Which of the following does performance monitoring primarily track over time?
options: Only whether each device is up or down
The user accounts that log on to each device
Utilization, error rates, and latency trends
The passwords and credentials used on the network
explain: Performance monitoring trends utilization, errors, and latency over time. Those trends reveal growing congestion and failing components and support capacity planning, unlike simple up/down status checks.

q: In a client-server model, what is the role of a client?
options: To passively store data for other hosts to retrieve
To forward packets between different networks
To provide services and resources to other hosts
To request services and resources from a server
explain: A client initiates requests for services — such as web pages, files, or email — and a server responds to those requests. This client-server model remains the dominant model on modern networks.

q: What is the main purpose of a deception grid (distributed honeynet)?
options: To provide additional production capacity during peak load
To attract legitimate users away from a busy server
To mirror production databases for backup purposes
To waste an attacker's time and reveal their tactics and techniques
explain: A deception grid deploys distributed decoy systems that no legitimate user should touch. Any interaction alerts defenders early and reveals the attacker's tactics, techniques, and procedures, especially during lateral movement.

q: An interface is stuck at 100 Mbps, half-duplex, while the connected device is set to full-duplex. What is the most likely cause?
options: A speed/duplex negotiation failure or hard-coded mismatch
A DNS server configuration error on the host
A faulty DHCP relay agent on the segment
An incorrect VLAN assignment on the switch port
explain: A link stuck at half-duplex at an unexpected speed usually means autonegotiation failed or one side was hard-coded while the other used auto. Verify both ends, ideally auto/auto, to restore full-duplex operation.

q: What should a metric retention policy define for monitoring data?
options: That all metrics are deleted at the end of each day
That all metrics are kept forever at full resolution
How long data is kept, balancing history needs against storage cost
That retention settings are left at each vendor's default
explain: A retention policy balances the value of historical data against storage cost — for example keeping granular recent data and rolling older data up into summaries instead of keeping everything forever or deleting it daily.

q: Why should firewall rule changes undergo peer review before implementation?
options: To delay changes so fewer changes are made each week
To satisfy a requirement that every change be tested in production first
To catch rule errors that could cause an outage or a security hole
To allow the reviewer to rewrite the change request in full
explain: A second set of eyes on firewall and ACL changes catches errors such as an overly broad permit or a wrong address object before the change can cause an outage or expose the network.

q: How does store-and-forward switching forward a frame?
options: It forwards the frame as soon as the destination MAC is read
It forwards the frame after reading only the first 64 bytes
It checks the entire frame for errors before forwarding it
It forwards the frame without checking any part of it
explain: A store-and-forward switch receives the whole frame and checks its CRC before forwarding. This adds latency but prevents errored frames from being propagated, unlike cut-through switching.

q: Users report packet loss only when the network is busy. What should a technician check first?
options: Whether DNS is resolving external hostnames correctly
Whether every interface is negotiating at full-duplex
Interface output drops for congestion and the QoS configuration
Whether the default gateway address is documented
explain: Packet loss under load with rising output drops points to congestion — the link or queue is full. The fix is more bandwidth, traffic shaping, or QoS that protects important traffic, not a cabling or DNS check.

q: A host can ping a server by IP address, but nslookup and dig fail to resolve names. What is the most likely problem?
options: A physical cable fault between the host and switch
A firewall blocking all ICMP echo traffic
A routing loop between the host and the server
A DNS server failure or incorrect DNS client configuration
explain: Successful ping by IP proves connectivity, so a name-resolution failure points to DNS — a down server or wrong DNS settings. Testing against a public resolver such as 8.8.8.8 helps separate a server fault from a client configuration fault.

q: Which sequence correctly shows OSPF neighbor states progressing toward a full adjacency?
options: Down, 2-Way, Full, ExStart, Exchange
Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, Full
Init, Down, 2-Way, Loading, Full, ExStart
2-Way, Down, Init, Full, Exchange, Loading
explain: OSPF neighbors move from Down through Init and 2-Way, then ExStart, Exchange, and Loading, before reaching Full, which means their link-state databases are synchronized.

q: What distinguishes an autonomous access point from a lightweight access point?
options: It must be managed by a wireless LAN controller
It functions as a wireless repeater for another AP
It can only operate as a client bridge to a controller
It operates standalone without requiring a controller
explain: An autonomous AP contains its full configuration and operates on its own, which suits small deployments. A lightweight AP, by contrast, depends on a controller for configuration and management.

q: How does a blue-green deployment release a new version of a service?
options: It updates servers in place one at a time during a maintenance window
It requires a scheduled downtime window to swap the code
It switches traffic between two parallel, identical environments
It deploys the new version to users without any fallback plan
explain: Blue-green deployment keeps two parallel environments. Traffic is switched from the old (blue) to the new (green) environment, so rollback is simply switching traffic back if problems appear.

q: What is a switch trunk port used for?
options: To carry traffic for multiple VLANs using 802.1Q tags
To carry traffic for a single untagged access VLAN
To connect a single desktop PC to the switch
To connect wireless clients to an access point
explain: A trunk port carries traffic for multiple VLANs between switches, routers, or APs, using 802.1Q tags to identify which VLAN each frame belongs to. An access port carries only one VLAN.

q: Which ICMP messages does the ping utility use?
options: Router advertisement and router solicitation messages
Redirect messages sent by a default gateway
Destination unreachable messages from a router
Echo request and echo reply messages
explain: Ping sends ICMP echo request messages and measures whether echo replies return and how long they take, which tests reachability and round-trip time.

q: When is a full packet capture most appropriate?
options: For routine billing of each department's bandwidth use
For continuous, always-on monitoring of all network traffic
As a replacement for system and application logs
For deep-dive analysis of a specific protocol or problem
explain: Packet capture shows the actual protocol exchanges, making it ideal for deep troubleshooting of a specific issue. It is used selectively because capturing everything does not scale for routine monitoring.

q: In DHCP, what do the letters in the DORA process stand for?
options: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge
Detect, Organize, Respond, Act
Dial, Open, Route, Accept
Data, Output, Return, Acknowledge
explain: DHCP leases use DORA: the client Discovers servers with a broadcast, a server Offers an address, the client Requests that address, and the server Acknowledges the lease.

q: How should a threat hunter form a hunting hypothesis?
options: By copying the alerts already generated by the SIEM
From threat intelligence and anomalies observed in the environment
By randomly selecting hosts to investigate each day
By reviewing only incidents that have already been closed
explain: Threat hunting is proactive: a hypothesis is built from threat intelligence and unusual patterns in the environment, then tested against data to find attacker tactics that alerts alone may have missed.

q: What problem can asymmetric routing cause in a network with stateful firewalls?
options: Stateful firewalls dropping traffic they never saw the start of
Stateful firewalls reordering packets so both paths appear as one flow
Faster traffic because return packets take a shorter path
Automatic load balancing across both firewall paths
explain: If return traffic bypasses the firewall that saw the outbound flow, that firewall has no state entry for it and drops it. Fixing path symmetry, so both directions cross the same firewall, resolves the drops.

q: What is the purpose of an automated rollback timer (such as reload-in) when changing a router remotely?
options: To revert the change automatically if it is not confirmed in time
To require an administrator to manually approve every command
To schedule the device to reboot at the same time every day
To prevent any configuration change from ever being saved
explain: A rollback timer restores the previous configuration if the administrator does not confirm the change within the set time. This protects against a change that locks the administrator out of the device.

q: What is the primary goal of change management?
options: To keep all network changes secret from end users
To make changes as quickly as possible without review
To prevent any changes to production systems
To make changes in a controlled way that minimizes risk
explain: Change management aims for controlled, low-risk changes — reviewed, documented, and with a backout plan — because unreviewed changes are a leading cause of outages.

q: Which type of address, used in IPv4, does NOT exist in IPv6?
options: Anycast, where one address reaches the nearest member of a group
Multicast, where one address reaches a group of hosts
Unicast, where one address identifies a single interface
Broadcast, replaced in IPv6 by multicast
explain: IPv6 has unicast, multicast, and anycast, but it eliminated broadcast. Functions that used broadcast in IPv4, such as neighbor discovery, use multicast in IPv6 instead.

q: What data rates and maximum distance is Category 8 cabling rated for?
options: 25/40 Gbps over distances up to 30 meters
100 Mbps over distances up to 100 meters
1 Gbps over distances up to 100 meters
10 Gbps over distances up to 100 meters
explain: Category 8 supports 25GBASE-T and 40GBASE-T, but only over short runs up to 30 meters, which makes it suited to data-center connections within or between nearby racks.

q: What special requirement applies to DFS channels in the 5 GHz band?
options: They may be used with no regulatory restrictions
They require radar detection and must be vacated if radar is detected
They are always available and never need to be changed
They operate in the 2.4 GHz band instead of 5 GHz
explain: Dynamic Frequency Selection channels are shared with radar systems. An AP using a DFS channel must detect radar and move to another channel if radar appears, to avoid interfering with it.

q: What does a self-healing network do when it detects a known fault?
options: It waits for an administrator to manually restart each device
It disables automation and raises a ticket for manual repair
It automatically remediates the fault, such as rerouting or restarting a port
It shuts down the affected segment until it is replaced
explain: Self-healing designs use event-driven automation to fix known faults without waiting for manual action — for example restarting a failed port or rerouting traffic around a failed link.

q: How does RSTP (802.1w) improve on the original Spanning Tree Protocol?
options: It converges more slowly to avoid making hasty decisions
It removes the need for redundant links in the topology
It converges in seconds instead of 30 to 50 seconds
It allows forwarding loops so traffic can use every link
explain: Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol converges in seconds, compared with roughly 30–50 seconds for classic STP, by using faster port states and proposal/agreement handshakes while still blocking loops.

q: What does a client-to-site (remote-access) VPN provide?
options: It joins two office networks together over the Internet
It operates with no software or configuration on the client
It is another name for a site-to-site VPN tunnel
It connects individual remote users to a central network
explain: A client-to-site VPN lets an individual remote user connect securely to the organization's network. A site-to-site VPN, by contrast, joins entire networks together.

q: How does fragment-free switching handle an incoming frame?
options: It checks the first 64 bytes to filter out collision fragments
It forwards the frame using wireless instead of wired media
It discards every frame shorter than the maximum frame size
It checks the entire frame exactly like store-and-forward switching
explain: Fragment-free switching reads the first 64 bytes — where collision fragments appear — before forwarding. It is a compromise that catches runts with lower latency than store-and-forward.

q: In order from the top layer down, what is the correct encapsulation sequence?
options: Data, segment, packet, frame, bits
Data, packet, segment, frame, bits
Bits, frame, packet, segment, data
Packet, segment, frame, bits, data
explain: As data moves down the stack, each layer adds its header: TCP creates a segment, IP creates a packet, Ethernet creates a frame, and the physical layer transmits bits.

q: What does a vendor support contract (such as Cisco SmartNet) typically provide?
options: Free hardware with no recurring contract cost
A guarantee that all support tickets are answered within five minutes
Optional coverage that always includes on-site cabling
Technical support (TAC) access and software updates
explain: A support contract provides access to the vendor's technical support center, software updates, and hardware replacement options. The coverage level should match how critical the device is.

q: What does mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) measure?
options: The time human resources takes to approve an on-call roster
The total time needed to fully resolve an incident (MTTR)
How quickly alerts are acknowledged by the responding team
The time needed to close an incident after it has been resolved
explain: MTTA is the average time between an alert being generated and a responder acknowledging it. It shows whether on-call and escalation processes are working, unlike MTTR, which measures full resolution.

q: A primary link repeatedly fails and recovers, causing constant failover and failback. How should this flapping be addressed?
options: Remove the backup link's preempt setting so the primary can never reclaim traffic
Tune the preempt/failback delay so failback waits for a stable primary
Disable the backup link so failover can never occur
Increase how often the device checks the primary link
explain: When a marginal primary link flaps, immediate failback causes repeated disruption. Adding a preempt or failback delay makes the device wait until the primary is stable before returning traffic to it.

q: What are the standard jacket colors for fiber patch cords?
options: Black for both single-mode and multimode fiber
Red for both single-mode and multimode fiber
Blue for both single-mode and multimode fiber
Yellow for single-mode and orange or aqua for multimode
explain: Fiber color codes help identify type at a glance: yellow indicates single-mode, orange indicates OM1/OM2 multimode, aqua indicates OM3/OM4 multimode, and lime green indicates OM5.

q: Wireless clients stay connected to a distant AP instead of roaming to a closer one. What helps fix these 'sticky' clients?
options: Creating a new SSID for clients to manually select
Enabling 802.11k/v/r assistance and disconnecting clients at very low RSSI
Lowering the data rates supported on the closer access points
Increasing transmit power on the distant access point
explain: Roaming assistance standards 802.11k, 802.11v, and 802.11r help clients find and move to better APs, and disconnecting clients below a minimum RSSI forces sticky clients to reassociate to a closer AP. Raising power usually makes the problem worse.

q: What does the address 0.0.0.0/0 represent in a routing table?
options: The address of the local host itself
An invalid entry that indicates a routing error
The default route that matches all destinations
The broadcast address for the local subnet
explain: 0.0.0.0/0 has a zero-length prefix, so it matches every destination. It is the default route — the gateway of last resort used when no more specific route matches.

q: OSPF neighbors are stuck in the Init or 2-Way state and never reach Full. What should be checked?
options: Whether the interfaces are assigned to the correct VLANs
Mismatched hello/dead timers, area, authentication, or an ACL blocking OSPF
Whether the links are operating at the fastest available speed
Whether DNS is resolving the neighbors' hostnames
explain: OSPF neighbors must agree on area, hello and dead timers, authentication, and related flags, and OSPF packets must not be blocked. A mismatch in any of these can leave neighbors stuck before Full.

q: What is the function of a network bridge?
options: To inspect and filter traffic like a stateful firewall
To forward frames between LAN segments based on MAC addresses
To amplify signals so they can travel longer distances
To route IP packets between different networks
explain: A bridge learns MAC addresses and forwards frames between two LAN segments, reducing unnecessary traffic. A bridge is essentially a two-port switch and operates at Layer 2, not as an IP router.

q: What is required to properly secure a server room (secure area)?
options: Leaving it open so administrators can enter quickly
Keeping it unlocked during business hours for convenience
Layered access controls such as locked doors, badges, and logging
Using the room primarily for general office storage
explain: Sensitive spaces need layered physical controls — locked doors and racks, badge or biometric access limited to authorized staff, and entry logging — rather than a single lock or open access.

q: What does a lightweight access point depend on a wireless LAN controller for?
options: Power, which it cannot receive from a PoE switch
Other access points, which provide its configuration
Wireless clients, which push configuration to the AP
Configuration and management, delivered over a CAPWAP tunnel
explain: A lightweight AP holds little configuration itself. It builds a CAPWAP tunnel to a wireless LAN controller, which provides its configuration, firmware, and centralized management.

q: How can VLAN hopping by double-tagging be prevented?
options: By using faster switches with higher port speeds
By creating a larger number of VLANs on the trunk
By setting the native VLAN to a dedicated, unused VLAN and tagging it
By encrypting all traffic carried on the trunk link
explain: Double-tagging exploits the native VLAN on a trunk. Using a dedicated native VLAN that carries no user traffic, and explicitly tagging it, removes the path the attack depends on.

q: What is the main benefit of Infrastructure as Code (IaC) for network configuration?
options: It makes rollback of a configuration change impossible
It applies changes more slowly than manual configuration
It requires every change to be typed manually at the CLI
It stores configurations as versioned code that can be reviewed and rolled back
explain: IaC treats network configuration like software: it is stored in version control, peer-reviewed, tested, and redeployed consistently, which makes rollback and auditing far easier than manual changes.

q: Why should unused services such as Telnet and HTTP be disabled on network devices?
options: Because unused services consume most of the device's CPU and memory
Because Telnet and HTTP are being removed from the TCP/IP standard
Because disabling them reduces the device's attack surface
Because disabling them will break all legitimate management access
explain: Every enabled service is a potential entry point. Disabling unused, especially cleartext, services such as Telnet and HTTP shrinks the attack surface and is a standard part of device hardening templates.

q: Which tools and functions rely on ICMP?
options: Ping and traceroute, which use echo and time-exceeded messages
File transfer protocols that move files between hosts
Email protocols that deliver mail between servers
Web protocols that retrieve pages from a server
explain: ICMP carries control and error messages for IP, including echo request/reply used by ping and time-exceeded messages used by traceroute, as well as destination unreachable messages.

q: What defines a connectionless protocol such as UDP or IP?
options: It guarantees delivery through acknowledgments and retransmission
It sends data without first setting up a connection
It requires a three-way handshake before sending data
It is always slower than any connection-oriented protocol
explain: A connectionless protocol sends data without a setup handshake and without delivery guarantees. That keeps overhead and latency low, which suits traffic such as DNS, voice, and streaming.

q: In which band does 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) operate, and what MIMO feature does it add?
options: 5 GHz, with MU-MIMO on the downlink
2.4 GHz only, with no MU-MIMO support
60 GHz, using millimeter-wave channels
6 GHz, using the Wi-Fi 6E band exclusively
explain: 802.11ac operates only in the 5 GHz band. It adds wider 80/160 MHz channels, 256-QAM, and downlink MU-MIMO (in Wave 2), unlike 802.11ad at 60 GHz or Wi-Fi 6E at 6 GHz.

q: How is an unstable, repeatedly advertised and withdrawn (flapping) BGP route handled?
options: Route dampening suppresses it until it becomes stable
The route is immediately withdrawn from every peer permanently
It is preferred over stable routes to speed convergence
It is automatically converted into a static route
explain: Route dampening penalizes a prefix each time it flaps and suppresses it until the penalty decays, which protects other routers from constant updates. The underlying cause of the flapping should still be fixed.

q: What does dependency mapping show in network operations?
options: Which services and devices fail when a given component fails
A list of optional features available in a monitoring tool
Only the physical cabling between devices in a rack
Only the applications installed on a single server
explain: A dependency map shows how services rely on devices and on each other. It predicts the blast radius of a failure and speeds triage by showing what else will be affected.

q: Why are physical badge access logs valuable to a security team?
options: They are used to calculate each employee's network bandwidth quota
They support physical investigations and timeline correlation
They are kept only to satisfy human resources requirements
They are routinely deleted so they cannot be reviewed
explain: Badge logs record who entered a secure area and when. Correlating them with network and system logs supports investigations of physical and cyber incidents.

q: How should an organization verify that its backups actually work?
options: By trusting that a successful backup job always restores
By checking only that the backup job reports no errors
By never testing restores to avoid disturbing production
By performing test restores to prove data can be recovered
explain: A backup is only proven by a successful restore. Regular test restores uncover silent failures — corrupt media, missing data, or wrong procedures — before a real recovery depends on them.

q: What does a crossover Ethernet cable do differently from a straight-through cable?
options: It is used to connect analog telephones to a PBX
It swaps the transmit and receive pairs between the two ends
It is a type of fiber-optic cable for long distances
It wires every pin straight through with no pairs swapped
explain: A crossover cable swaps the transmit and receive pairs, which allowed two similar devices to communicate directly. Modern Auto-MDIX ports detect and adjust automatically, so crossover cables are rarely needed.

q: What is a dual-homed (multihomed) host, and why can it be a concern?
options: A host that acts as a dedicated hardware firewall
A host whose second interface is reserved only for out-of-band management
A host with two network interfaces, which could bridge two networks if routing is enabled
A host that requires no configuration on either interface
explain: A dual-homed host connects to two networks through separate interfaces. If IP forwarding or routing is enabled on it, it can bridge those networks and bypass security controls, so forwarding should be disabled unless it is intended.

q: How should firewall rule bloat be managed over time?
options: By regularly auditing rules and removing unused or shadowed ones
By exporting the rule base to a spreadsheet once a year
By adding a new rule for every request without reviewing old ones
By assuming extra rules increase security by adding complexity
explain: Over time, unused, duplicate, and shadowed firewall rules accumulate risk and make reviews harder. Regular audits that remove or correct those rules keep the rule base effective.

q: What does a DNS A record map?
options: A domain name to the mail servers for that domain
A hostname to an IPv6 address for dual-stack hosts
An IP address back to a hostname in a reverse zone
A hostname to an IPv4 address
explain: An A record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address. A AAAA record maps to IPv6, an MX record identifies mail servers, and a PTR record maps an IP address back to a hostname.

q: What are the typical symptoms of a duplex mismatch on a link?
options: Collisions, CRC errors, and very slow throughput
Much faster speeds than the link is rated for
Improved security because the link runs at half-duplex
No symptoms; both sides perform as if correctly configured
explain: With one side at full-duplex and the other at half-duplex, the half-duplex side treats simultaneous traffic as collisions, producing late collisions, CRC errors, and poor throughput.

q: What does DHCP snooping build on a switch?
options: A binding table mapping IP addresses to MAC addresses and ports
A routing table for directing traffic between VLANs
A list of VLANs configured on trunk ports
A MIB describing every managed object on the switch
explain: DHCP snooping records legitimate leases in a binding table of IP address, MAC address, VLAN, and switch port. That database is then used by Dynamic ARP Inspection and IP Source Guard.

q: How should network device configuration backups be handled?
