options: They should be automated, versioned, and stored off the device
They should be taken manually only after a failure occurs
They should never be taken so old settings cannot return
They should be stored only on the device that was backed up
explain: Automated, versioned backups stored off-device make recovery after a failure or bad change fast and make it possible to audit exactly what changed and when.

q: Why is an accurate, documented network map important for troubleshooting?
options: It is a reference used mainly when designing a brand-new network
It is mainly useful to external auditors after an incident
It quickly becomes inaccurate and should not be relied on
It is a primary troubleshooting reference for topology and connections
explain: A current network map shows topology, addressing, and connections, so a technician can trace a path and isolate a fault quickly. Troubleshooting without one is largely guesswork.

q: How is a rogue DHCP server on a LAN most reliably located?
options: By rebooting every switch on the affected segment
By checking DNS records for the rogue server's hostname
By using DHCP snooping logs and a packet capture to find its MAC and port
By guessing which workstation is most likely running it
explain: DHCP snooping flags DHCP offers on untrusted ports, and a packet capture reveals the rogue server's MAC address and switch port, so it can be found and removed with evidence rather than by rebooting or guessing.

q: Name resolution is slow for every user on the network. What should be checked?
options: The cabling of a single user's workstation
The client settings on one affected workstation
The DNS server's health, load, and its forwarders
The switch ports connecting the printers
explain: When DNS is slow for everyone, the shared service is the suspect: check the DNS server's health and query response times and whether its forwarders are responding, rather than individual clients or cabling.

q: Spanning Tree is blocking a port that should be forwarding. What should be checked?
options: Root bridge placement, bridge priorities, and port costs
The duplex settings on the blocked port's link partner
Whether the block is improving performance and should stay
Whether cable lengths exceed the maximum for the media type
explain: Unexpected STP blocking usually means the root bridge is in the wrong place or priorities and path costs lead to a suboptimal topology. Correcting root placement and costs restores the intended forwarding path.

q: What does intermittent (on-and-off) connectivity most often indicate?
options: A physical-layer problem such as bad cabling, EMI, or a duplex mismatch
A firewall rule that permanently blocks the traffic
A routing loop that forwards packets indefinitely
A DNS problem that affects only name resolution
explain: Intermittent loss that comes and goes usually has a physical cause — damaged cabling, electromagnetic interference, failing optics, or a duplex mismatch — rather than a permanent firewall or DNS fault.

q: What is a maintenance window?
options: An unplanned outage caused by a failed change
A notification sent to users after work is finished
A type of monitoring alert for high utilization
A scheduled period of downtime reserved for making changes
explain: A maintenance window is scheduled, announced downtime set aside for disruptive work such as upgrades or reconfiguration, so users and support teams know what to expect.

q: What does a media converter most commonly connect?
options: A coaxial network to a DSL Internet connection
A USB device to an HDMI display input
A wireless network to a Bluetooth device
Copper Ethernet to a fiber-optic link
explain: A media converter translates between media types, most commonly copper Ethernet and fiber, which lets a copper LAN be extended over fiber distances without replacing the switches.

q: What does SLAAC allow an IPv6 host to do?
options: Continue using only IPv4 addressing on the network
Configure its own IPv6 address using router advertisements
Operate without any address configuration at all
Require a DHCPv6 server for every address it uses
explain: Stateless Address Autoconfiguration lets an IPv6 host build its own address from the prefix in a router advertisement plus its interface identifier, without needing a DHCPv6 server to assign it.

q: A DHCP scope is exhausted. What symptom will new clients show?
options: They will be unable to obtain a lease and will assign themselves an APIPA address
They will receive a DNS error when browsing the web
They will slow down traffic for every existing client
They will cause all existing clients to lose their leases
explain: When no leases remain, a new client gets no DHCP reply and self-assigns an APIPA address in 169.254.0.0/16, so it cannot reach other subnets. Expanding the scope or shortening lease times resolves it.

q: What does a VLAN segment on a switch?
options: Wide area networks at different branch locations
Broadcast domains, logically, on shared switch hardware
Collision domains, by physically separating every host
Electrical power domains for Power over Ethernet devices
explain: A VLAN logically divides a switch into separate broadcast domains, isolating traffic between groups without needing separate physical switches or hardware.

q: UDP port 161 is used by which service?
options: TFTP, for transferring configuration files
SNMP, for polling managed network devices
DNS, for resolving hostnames to addresses
NTP, for synchronizing device clocks
explain: SNMP managers poll agents on UDP port 161 to collect status and performance data, and agents send traps to a manager on UDP port 162.

q: What characterizes a protocol-based DDoS attack, such as a SYN flood?
options: It attacks only the application layer of a single server
It exhausts connection state tables by opening many half-open sessions
It floods a link purely by sending maximum-bandwidth traffic
It relies on users voluntarily installing malicious software
explain: Protocol attacks exploit state: a SYN flood fills a device's connection table with half-open sessions so legitimate connections cannot be established. SYN cookies and rate limiting help blunt this type of attack.

q: What is the purpose of license management for network systems?
options: To track software used only on end-user desktops
To negotiate volume discounts with software resellers
To track entitlements, usage, and renewal dates
It is needed only when a vendor requests an audit
explain: License management tracks what the organization is entitled to use and when licenses renew. An expired license can disable features or support, so renewal dates must be calendared.

q: What is the purpose of log aggregation?
options: To delete local logs so devices have more storage
To compress events so each device stores a full year of logs locally
To slow down devices so they generate fewer events
To centralize events so they can be correlated and searched together
explain: Log aggregation collects events from many devices into one platform, such as a SIEM, where they can be correlated across sources to reveal incidents that a single device's log would not show.

q: What do syslog facility and severity values do?
options: They slow logging so a busy device is not overwhelmed
They indicate that a log message has been encrypted
They select which log messages are encrypted in transit
They categorize the message source and prioritize its urgency
explain: Syslog uses a facility to identify the source type (such as kernel or authentication) and a severity from 0 (emergency) to 7 (debug) to indicate urgency, which structures filtering and alerting.

q: Why should BGP peering sessions use authentication such as MD5 or TCP-AO?
options: It is required only for internal BGP (iBGP) sessions
To protect the session from unauthorized peering and hijacking attempts
Because authentication is enabled by default on all BGP sessions
Because unauthenticated sessions cannot exchange any routes
explain: Authenticating a BGP session ensures routes are exchanged only with the intended peer and protects the TCP session from spoofing or hijacking. It is not on by default and should be configured, especially for external peers.

q: A VPN peer's public IP address is dynamic and has just changed, breaking the tunnel. What addresses this?
options: Renegotiating the IKE Phase 1 keys so the tunnel relearns the peer's new address
Using DDNS for the peer hostname, or a mode designed for dynamic peers
Switching the tunnel to IKEv1 main mode so it can accept a changing peer address
Pointing the tunnel configuration at the peer's private LAN address
explain: If a peer's address changes, a tunnel configured for a fixed IP will fail. Pointing the configuration at a Dynamic DNS hostname that follows the peer, or using a mode that accepts dynamic peers, restores the tunnel.

q: During a network incident, what does NetFlow data most quickly reveal?
options: Which hosts are the top talkers and any anomalous traffic flows
Billing totals for each department's Internet use
Which users are due for a password change this week
The exact packet payloads sent by each application
explain: NetFlow summarizes who is talking to whom, on which ports, and how much. During an incident it identifies the top talkers and anomalous flows in seconds, though it does not contain packet payloads.

q: A user cannot reach a remote subnet, and the gateway returns 'destination unreachable'. What does this indicate?
options: A missing route, so the gateway has no path to that subnet
A VLAN mismatch on the user's access switch port
A link that is reachable but responding slowly to ping
A DNS failure preventing the hostname from resolving
explain: A destination unreachable message from the gateway means it has no route to that network. Check routing tables on each hop and add a static route or fix the routing protocol.

q: A packet capture shows a large storm of TCP RST packets. What does this most likely suggest?
options: A single host repeatedly rebooting and re-establishing its session
A port scan, or applications abruptly closing many sessions
A switch loop flooding the segment with broadcast traffic
A DNS server returning incorrect records to clients
explain: Many RST packets in a short period are abnormal — they commonly indicate a port scan probing closed ports, or faulty applications brutally closing sessions instead of completing a normal close.

q: TCP port 3389 is used by which service?
options: VNC, for remote framebuffer access to a desktop
Telnet, for cleartext remote terminal access
RDP, for Microsoft Remote Desktop access
SSH, for secure remote terminal access
explain: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) listens on TCP port 3389. By comparison, SSH uses port 22, Telnet uses port 23, and VNC typically uses port 5900.

q: Wireless clients cannot connect to the WLAN at all. What should be checked first?
options: Whether the wired Internet connection is working
Whether DNS is resolving external hostnames
Whether the core routers have the latest firmware
The SSID, the pre-shared key, and the clients' signal strength
explain: Start with the basics of association: that the correct SSID is visible, the pre-shared key or credentials are correct, and the client has adequate signal strength, before investigating Internet, DNS, or routing faults.

q: What is the core principle of a zero-trust security model?
options: Every access request is explicitly verified using identity and context
Authenticated users require no further checks inside the network
Zero trust can be achieved by purchasing a single product
Devices on the internal LAN are trusted by default
explain: Zero trust means never trust, always verify: every access request is authenticated and authorized using identity and context, regardless of whether it originates inside or outside the network perimeter.

q: What is the difference between fail-closed and fail-open behavior in an IPS?
options: Fail-open blocks traffic on failure, while fail-closed passes it
Both settings block all traffic when the device fails
Fail-closed blocks traffic on failure (more secure); fail-open passes it (more available)
Fail-closed applies to IPS devices, while fail-open applies only to firewalls
explain: If an IPS fails closed, it blocks traffic, favoring security over availability. If it fails open, it passes traffic, favoring availability. The choice depends on the risk the organization accepts.

q: Monitoring alerts for a link repeatedly trigger and clear within minutes. What is needed?
options: Disable monitoring on the link until the alerts stop occurring
Wider use of the same threshold so more alerts are generated
Immediate replacement of the monitored device in all cases
Alert dampening thresholds (hysteresis) so a flapping state does not spam alerts
explain: Flapping alerts are tamed with dampening — for example requiring a condition to persist, or to clear for a set time, before alerting again. This hysteresis stops a marginal link from flooding responders.

q: What does a divide-and-conquer troubleshooting approach do?
options: It replaces every component in the path at the same time
It isolates the fault domain by systematically testing the middle of the path
It tests components in a random order until the fault is found
It is a guess-based method with no systematic testing
explain: Divide and conquer bisects the path between client and server — test the midpoint, then the midpoint of the failing half — halving the search space at each step until the fault domain is isolated.

q: How is a blind spot in network monitoring coverage discovered?
options: By auditing monitoring coverage against the actual device inventory
By assuming every critical device is already monitored
Attackers revealing it is the only way it is ever found
Only by waiting for a monitored device to fail and tracing the outage
explain: A blind spot is found by regularly auditing coverage — comparing the inventory of critical devices and links against what is actually monitored — so gaps are closed before an incident hides in one.

q: What is a network darknet (telescope) used for?
options: To carry production traffic over unused dark fiber
To provide Internet access to users in a secure area
To encrypt traffic between two production data centers
To monitor unused IP address space for scanning and unsolicited traffic
explain: A darknet monitors address space that hosts no legitimate services. Any traffic arriving there is unsolicited — usually scanning or misconfiguration — which reveals reconnaissance campaigns early.

q: What is a gratuitous ARP (GARP) message?
options: An ARP announcement a host sends unprompted for its own IP address
An ARP request a host sends for the gateway's address at boot
A DNS query a host sends to resolve its own hostname
A message that is always evidence of a malicious attack
explain: A gratuitous ARP is an unsolicited announcement of a host's own IP-to-MAC mapping. It updates neighbors' caches and helps detect duplicate IP addresses, although the same mechanism can be abused for spoofing.

q: What do NTP stratum numbers indicate?
options: The security level assigned to each time server
How far a time source is from the reference clock, with lower being more accurate
A random value assigned when the server is installed
The number of clients currently syncing to the server
explain: NTP stratum ranks time sources: stratum 0 is a reference clock such as an atomic clock, stratum 1 servers connect directly to it, and each higher stratum is one step further away and slightly less accurate.

q: What is iPerf used to measure?
options: How quickly a DNS server answers a query
Whether a host responds to an ICMP ping
The actual throughput (bandwidth) achieved over a link
Whether an email server accepts a test message
explain: iPerf generates controlled traffic between two endpoints and measures the real throughput achieved, which isolates link bandwidth from application behavior such as slow servers or DNS delays.

q: What distinguishes an SSL/TLS VPN from a traditional IPsec remote-access VPN?
options: It requires a dedicated thick client on every device
It tunnels its traffic inside an IPsec ESP session in transport mode
It can work through a web browser without installed client software
It provides no encryption for the traffic it carries
explain: An SSL/TLS (clientless) VPN tunnels access through HTTPS in a browser, so users need no installed VPN client and the traffic passes easily through most firewalls.

q: What do excessive collisions on a half-duplex segment suggest?
options: That too many stations on the segment are using jumbo frames
That CSMA/CD has been disabled on the segment's devices
That the segment is carrying an unusually small amount of traffic
That the shared media is overloaded, or a duplex problem exists
explain: Collisions should be rare on a lightly loaded half-duplex segment and absent on modern full-duplex links. Excessive collisions point to overloaded shared media or a duplex mismatch that needs correction.

q: An IPsec tunnel is up, but no traffic passes through it, and the traffic selectors (proxy IDs) do not match. What is the result and fix?
options: No traffic will pass until the selectors are made to mirror each other exactly
The tunnel will pass traffic once Phase 1 renegotiates the selectors
The mismatch matters only for multicast traffic, not for unicast traffic
Traffic will be routed around the tunnel automatically
explain: On a policy-based VPN, the traffic selectors or proxy IDs on each side must mirror each other exactly. If they do not, the tunnel can appear up while passing no traffic until they are corrected.

q: What does end-user experience monitoring measure?
options: Performance as experienced from the client's perspective, including synthetic transactions
Advertising click-through rates for a public website
Performance measured only from inside the server itself
A metric that only reports whether a server port is open
explain: End-user experience monitoring tests performance from where the user sits — often with synthetic transactions that mimic real tasks — so it catches problems that server-side metrics alone would miss.

q: At which layer of the OSI model do switches primarily operate?
options: Layer 1, the Physical layer
Layer 2, the Data Link layer
Layer 7, the Application layer
Layer 3, the Network layer
explain: A switch forwards frames based on MAC addresses, which is a Layer 2 (Data Link) function. Layer 3 devices such as routers forward packets based on IP addresses.

q: What does DMVPN allow branch (spoke) sites to do?
options: Operate without any hub router in the design
Replace the hub-and-spoke design with a full mesh of permanent tunnels
Build dynamic, direct spoke-to-spoke VPN tunnels as needed
Use only permanent, static tunnels through the hub for all traffic
explain: Dynamic Multipoint VPN uses a hub with mGRE and NHRP so spokes can build direct tunnels to each other on demand, instead of hairpinning all spoke-to-spoke traffic through the hub.

q: What is a time-domain reflectometer (TDR) used to find?
options: The maximum data rate a cable can support
The usable bandwidth of a copper cable run
The distance to a cable fault such as an open or short
The location of a break in a fiber-optic cable
explain: A TDR sends a pulse down a copper cable and times the reflection to calculate the distance to a fault such as an open or short. A fiber break is located with the optical equivalent, an OTDR.

q: What is the role of a source of truth such as NetBox in network automation?
options: To provide DNS name resolution for automated devices
To store backup copies of running configurations only
To hold manually updated spreadsheets for each site
To serve as the authoritative inventory of the intended network state
explain: Automation tools read the intended state of the network from the source of truth, so changes are driven by one authoritative inventory instead of drifting spreadsheets or ad hoc records.

q: What does dynamic NAT do when an inside host starts a session to the Internet?
options: It maps the inside host to one permanent public address reserved for that host
It assigns the inside host an available public address from a NAT pool
It translates many inside hosts to a single public address using different ports
It forwards the traffic without changing the source address
explain: Dynamic NAT assigns a public address from a configured pool on demand and releases it when the session ends. A permanent one-to-one mapping is static NAT, and sharing one address by ports is PAT.

q: A copper cable run shows intermittent errors near an equipment room. Which of the following is a common source of electromagnetic interference (EMI) the technician should check for?
options: The DHCP lease time configured on the server
The fiber-optic backbone cable feeding the wiring closet
Fluorescent lights, electric motors, and microwave ovens near the run
The VLAN assignment configured on the access switch
explain: Fluorescent lighting, motors, and microwaves generate EMI that can corrupt signals on copper cabling. Keeping copper away from these sources, or using shielded cable in noisy areas, reduces the errors.

q: How does an iterative DNS query work?
options: The first server contacted resolves the full name on the client's behalf
The root server returns the final address record directly to the client
Each server returns the final answer without referring the client elsewhere
Each server returns a referral, and the resolver follows the referrals down the chain
explain: In an iterative query, root and TLD servers do not finish the lookup; they return referrals to servers closer to the answer, and the resolver follows those referrals until it reaches the authoritative server.

q: What is a looking glass server used for?
options: To inspect traffic mirrored from a production link
To store backup copies of router configurations
To view a provider's routing table and test reachability from the provider's perspective
To assign IP addresses to hosts on a provider's network
explain: A looking glass lets you run limited route and ping checks from a provider's routers, so you can see how your prefixes and destinations look from outside your own network.

q: Which of the following describes the best practice for device configuration backups?
options: Backups are run manually and stored only on each device itself
Backups run automatically to secure off-device storage with version history
Backups are copied to a public file share without access controls
Backups are taken once at installation and never updated afterward
explain: Scheduled, automated backups stored off the device, with older versions kept, let you restore a known configuration after a failure or a bad change. A copy that lives only on the failed device is useless.

q: What do DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) provide?
options: They authenticate DNS responses by signing the zone data
They replace DNS servers by broadcasting queries on the local network
They encrypt DNS queries between the client and the resolver
They cache DNS records so that queries never leave the local network
explain: DoH and DoT encrypt the query itself, using HTTPS or TLS, so observers on the path cannot snoop on the names being looked up. Signing zone data for authentication is DNSSEC, a different protection.

q: What is the difference between a bit and a baud?
options: A bit is an analog waveform, and baud is a digital data unit
A bit is the number of signal changes per second, and baud is the amount of data transferred
A bit is a unit of data, and baud is the number of signal changes per second
A bit and a baud always represent exactly the same amount of information
explain: Bits measure data, while baud measures how many times the signal changes each second. Advanced modulation can encode several bits in each signal change, so the bit rate can be higher than the baud rate.

q: What security concern applies to proxy Neighbor Discovery (proxy NDP) in IPv6?
options: It encrypts neighbor discovery so switches cannot inspect the traffic
It can be abused for neighbor spoofing, in much the same way as proxy ARP
It removes the need to perform duplicate address detection
It operates only on IPv4 networks and ignores IPv6 traffic
explain: A device answering neighbor discovery on behalf of others can be impersonated or abused to redirect traffic, just as with proxy ARP in IPv4. IPv6 neighbor discovery therefore needs the same first-hop protections.

q: What geographic scope does a metropolitan area network (MAN) cover?
options: A city or metropolitan area
A single room or a personal work area
A single building or a small office
Multiple countries across the globe
explain: A MAN links sites across a city or metro area, which is larger than a single-building LAN and smaller than a wide area network spanning countries.

q: What does a normal change require before it is implemented?
options: Implementation as quickly as possible with no documented review
Approval from the end users of every affected service
Pre-approval as a standard change, with no further review needed
Risk assessment, formal approval, and scheduling
explain: A normal change follows the full change process: it is assessed for risk and impact, approved (often by a change advisory board), and scheduled. Pre-approved changes are standard changes, and unscheduled urgent handling is for emergency changes.

q: A packet capture shows a large number of TCP retransmissions on a connection. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The link has high latency but is delivering every packet on the first attempt
Packets are being lost or arriving out of order along the path
The application data is being encrypted before transmission
The receiver is sending window updates more frequently than expected
explain: TCP retransmits segments that were not acknowledged, so frequent retransmissions point to packet loss or reordering caused by congestion, duplex problems, or a failing link.

q: During an outage, when can a temporary static route be useful?
options: As a permanent replacement for the dynamic routing protocol
To advertise a backup path to a neighboring autonomous system
To summarize dynamically learned routes into a single announcement
To bypass a failed dynamically learned path until that path is repaired
explain: A temporary static route can bridge traffic around a broken dynamic path while you repair it. It should be removed once normal routing is restored so it does not become a forgotten, stale entry.

q: What does a security baseline audit do?
options: It simulates an attacker attempting to exploit vulnerabilities
It checks only whether the organization holds a compliance certificate
It scans the network for active malware infections
It compares device configurations against approved hardening standards
explain: A baseline audit measures current configurations against the approved hardening guide and flags drift from the secure standard. Simulating an attacker is a penetration test, which is a different activity.

q: What does the term 'single pane of glass' mean in network monitoring?
options: A single physical monitor must be used in the network operations center
Monitoring data from multiple tools is unified in one consolidated view
All network devices must be managed from a single vendor's platform
Alerts are displayed in one place but cannot be correlated across systems
explain: A single pane of glass brings metrics, alerts, and status from many tools into one correlated dashboard, so staff do not have to hop between separate consoles during an incident.

q: What is the IPv6 loopback address?
explain: ::1 is the IPv6 loopback address, equivalent to 127.0.0.1 in IPv4. ff02::1 is the all-nodes multicast address, and fe80::/10 addresses are link-local.

q: What is the first step of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology?
options: Escalate the issue to the vendor
Implement the most likely solution
Identify the problem
Document the findings and outcomes
explain: The methodology starts with identifying the problem, then establishes a theory, tests it, plans and implements a solution, verifies functionality, and finally documents. Skipping identification leads to fixing the wrong thing.

q: A technician is using a top-down troubleshooting approach on a problem that appears to be an application error. Where does this approach start?
options: At the Physical layer of the OSI model
At the Data Link layer of the OSI model
At the Application layer of the OSI model
At the Network layer of the OSI model
explain: Top-down troubleshooting starts at Layer 7, the Application layer, and works downward. It fits cases where the lower layers are known to be working, such as an app error on a healthy link.

q: What defines a socket for a network connection endpoint?
options: The MAC address and VLAN ID of the host
The hostname and domain name of the host
The IP address, port number, and transport protocol
The IP address and MAC address of the host only
explain: A socket is identified by an IP address, a port number, and the protocol in use. That combination uniquely identifies one endpoint of a connection on a host that may run many services.

q: How are users typically authenticated in a WPA2-Enterprise wireless network?
options: With a shared passphrase that all users know
By filtering the MAC addresses of client devices
By a RADIUS server using 802.1X and EAP for per-user authentication
With WPS using a PIN or push-button enrollment
explain: WPA2-Enterprise authenticates each user individually through 802.1X/EAP against a RADIUS server, so there is no shared passphrase to leak or rotate for everyone.

q: What characterizes a connection-oriented protocol such as TCP?
options: It sends data without any setup and provides no delivery guarantees
It broadcasts its data to all hosts on the local segment
It prioritizes low delay over reliable, ordered delivery
It establishes a session before transferring data
explain: Connection-oriented protocols set up a session first, as TCP does with its three-way handshake. That setup overhead buys sequencing, acknowledgments, and reliable, ordered delivery.

q: How many layers does the TCP/IP model have?
options: Five layers
Seven layers
Three layers
Four layers
explain: The TCP/IP model has four layers: Network Access, Internet, Transport, and Application. The seven-layer model is the OSI model.

q: A BGP session will not move past the Active and Connect states. What is the most likely cause?
options: TCP port 179 is blocked or the peer is misconfigured
The two routers are exchanging the full routing table too slowly
The local LAN switch is experiencing a spanning-tree topology change
The local router's BGP router ID conflicts with its OSPF router ID
explain: BGP peers over TCP port 179, so a session stuck in Active/Connect usually means that connection is blocked or a setting such as the remote AS or password does not match on the two sides.

q: What is the purpose of a red team exercise?
options: To audit configurations against a compliance checklist
To patch the vulnerabilities found by a vulnerability scanner
To emulate a real adversary's tactics to test detection and response
To train new employees on the organization's security policies
explain: A red team behaves like a real attacker, using realistic tactics over time, which tests whether the organization can detect, respond to, and contain an intrusion, not just whether a checklist item exists.

q: Approximately how much overhead does IPsec add to a packet?
options: No additional bytes at all
About 5 to 10 bytes per packet
About 500 bytes per packet
About 50 to 70 bytes per packet
explain: IPsec ESP headers, trailers, and integrity data typically add roughly 50 to 70 bytes, depending on mode and algorithms. That shrinks the effective MTU, so MTU and fragmentation need to be planned for on IPsec links.

q: What information is recorded in a switch's DHCP snooping binding table for each client?
options: The client's MAC address, leased IP address, VLAN, and switch port
The client's hostname, user account, and directory group membership
The client's public IP address and NAT port for each outbound session
The default gateway and DNS servers offered in each DHCP lease
explain: The binding table records which MAC and IP addresses were legitimately leased, on which VLAN and port. Features such as Dynamic ARP Inspection and IP Source Guard validate traffic against this table.

q: What is a broadcast domain?
options: The set of devices that share the same collision domain
The set of devices assigned to the same DNS zone
The set of devices connected to the public Internet
The set of devices that receive one another's broadcast frames
explain: A broadcast domain is the group of devices that hear each other's broadcasts. Routers bound broadcast domains, and VLANs segment them within a switched network.

q: An analyst cannot read the encrypted payloads in a capture. What can the analyst still examine to investigate the traffic?
options: The plaintext contents of the application data
The private encryption keys of the users involved
The exact commands sent inside each TLS session
Metadata such as addresses, ports, timing, and packet sizes
explain: Even when payloads are encrypted, flow metadata such as endpoints, ports, timing, sizes, and TLS handshake fingerprints still reveals a great deal about what a host is doing and with whom.

q: What do ICMP Destination Unreachable messages in a packet capture indicate?
options: The destination is accepting traffic on all of its ports
ICMP is being used to transfer files between the hosts
A host or port is unreachable, or the traffic is being filtered
Packets are reaching the destination by the fastest available route
explain: Destination Unreachable messages, with codes for host, port, or filtered traffic, show exactly where and why packets are being rejected, which helps map firewall and routing problems.

q: How many layers does the OSI reference model have?
options: Eight layers
Four layers
Seven layers
Five layers
explain: The OSI model has seven layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application. The four-layer model is the TCP/IP model.

q: What should a technician verify when troubleshooting a cable modem with intermittent connectivity?
options: Whether the modem supports VLAN tagging on its LAN ports
Whether the modem's MAC address table has aged out correctly
Whether the downstream and upstream power levels and the SNR are within specification
Whether the modem is running the latest routing protocol software
explain: Cable modems need downstream/upstream RF power and signal-to-noise ratio within the provider's specification. Out-of-spec levels from bad splitters or signal ingress cause drops and slow speeds.

q: A long copper run is failing because of attenuation. Which action best fixes the problem?
options: Reboot the switch at the far end of the run
Shorten the run or install a switch or repeater to regenerate the signal
Install faster network adapters at both ends of the run
Move the link into a different VLAN on the switch
explain: Attenuation grows with distance, and Ethernet copper runs are limited to about 100 meters. Shortening the run, or breaking it with an intermediate switch or a fiber segment, restores the signal.

q: What address range does the private block 172.16.0.0/12 span?
explain: A /12 mask fixes the first 12 bits, so the second octet can range from 16 to 31. The private block is therefore 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255.

q: What advantage does the 6 GHz band provide for Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7?
options: Longer range than the 2.4 GHz band through walls
Backward compatibility with 2.4 GHz-only client devices
Reuse of the most congested 5 GHz channels
Additional, relatively clean spectrum that supports wide channels
explain: The 6 GHz band adds a large amount of previously unused spectrum, allowing wide channels with far less congestion from legacy devices. Its range is shorter than 2.4 GHz, not longer.

q: In IPv6, what is a /64 prefix typically used for?
options: A point-to-point host route to a single device
The standard prefix size for a LAN subnet
A multicast group address range
The loopback address on a host
explain: A /64 leaves 64 bits for the interface identifier and is the standard subnet size for IPv6 LANs. SLAAC depends on /64, so smaller LAN prefixes break automatic address configuration.

q: How is networking commonly implemented for containers and Kubernetes pods?
options: Through overlay networks and container network interface (CNI) plugins
Through hubs that place all containers in one collision domain
Through one permanently assigned physical NIC for each container
Through static ARP entries configured manually on each host
explain: Container platforms use CNI plugins such as Calico or Flannel to connect pods, often over an overlay network. This provides pod-to-pod addressing and policy without wiring each container to physical hardware.

q: What is the main role of the distribution layer in a three-tier network design?
options: To connect end-user devices directly to the network
To aggregate access-layer traffic and apply routing and policy
To provide the fastest possible backbone transport between buildings
To assign IP addresses to clients through DHCP
explain: The distribution layer aggregates the access layer and is where routing, ACLs, and QoS policy are commonly applied. Connecting end devices is the access layer's job, and high-speed transport is the core's.

q: What does an IP address management (IPAM) tool primarily track?
options: Wireless channel utilization across access points
User authentication events on the directory server
Physical cable certification results for each run
The allocation and use of IP address space
explain: IPAM keeps a central record of which subnets and addresses are allocated, reserved, and free. That documentation prevents address conflicts and makes capacity planning possible.

q: Users can reach websites by IP address but not by name. What is the most likely cause?
options: An incorrect default gateway configured on the clients
A failed uplink on the access switch serving the clients
Excessive latency on the WAN link to the provider
Incorrect DNS server addresses configured on the clients
explain: If IP connectivity works but name resolution fails, the problem is in DNS, most often wrong resolver addresses on the clients. Tools such as nslookup or dig isolate name resolution from general connectivity.

q: What is a shadowed firewall rule?
options: A rule that can never match because an earlier rule already handles the same traffic
A rule saved as a backup and left disabled until it is needed
A rule that only logs traffic without allowing or denying it
A rule that is configured only on the standby firewall
explain: Because firewalls evaluate rules in order and act on the first match, a later rule covering the same traffic is shadowed and can never take effect. Rule audits flag these so the policy stays understandable.

q: Why would a technician use conditional debugging on a production router?
options: To send debug output to every terminal session at once
To limit debug output to the traffic or interfaces relevant to the problem
To run debug commands without consuming any CPU resources
To convert debug messages into SNMP traps for the NMS
explain: Unfiltered debugs can overwhelm a production router's CPU. Conditioning the debug on an interface or access list shows only the relevant events and keeps the device safe to run.

q: What does the attenuation-to-crosstalk ratio (ACR) of a copper cable indicate?
options: The amount of usable signal headroom once crosstalk is taken into account
The maximum data rate printed in the cable category specification
The amount of signal lost purely because of the cable's length
The amount of electromagnetic interference the cable itself generates
explain: ACR compares the wanted signal, after attenuation, with the crosstalk noise on the pair. A healthy positive margin means the signal stands clear of the noise and the link should perform reliably.

q: What does SNMPv3 in authPriv mode provide?
options: Authentication and encryption of SNMP management messages
Cleartext community-string access, as in SNMPv2c
Authentication of messages with no encryption of their contents
Read-only access using the default 'public' community string
explain: authPriv is the highest SNMPv3 security level: messages are authenticated and encrypted, unlike community strings in v1/v2c, which travel in cleartext. authNoPriv authenticates but does not encrypt.

q: A site survey identifies areas of weak wireless signal in an office. Which action best addresses the problem?
options: Increase the transmit power of every access point to maximum
Replace all of the client devices in the weak areas with newer models
Move the affected users to desks that already have stronger coverage
Reposition existing access points or add access points based on the survey results
explain: Weak coverage is a placement problem, so the fix is survey-driven: move APs or add APs where coverage is thin. Simply raising power can increase interference and does not fix dead spots predictably.

q: What is certificate pinning?
options: Installing a CA certificate in a browser's trust store
Using a self-signed certificate on an internal server
Revoking a certificate before its scheduled expiration date
Configuring an app to expect a specific certificate or public key for a server
explain: Pinning hard-codes the expected certificate or public key in the application, so it rejects even a validly issued but unexpected certificate. This defeats many man-in-the-middle attacks but makes certificate rotation harder.

q: When sizing a UPS for a network closet, which factors are most important?
options: The total cable length in the closet and the height of the rack
The number of USB ports and management features on the UPS
The total connected load in watts and the runtime required
The brand of the power distribution units installed in the rack
explain: UPS sizing starts with the combined wattage of the equipment it must carry and how long it must run, for example long enough for a graceful shutdown or for a generator to start.

q: What does network access control (NAC) do?
options: It inspects Internet traffic at the network perimeter
It checks a device's compliance and controls its admission before granting network access
It encrypts traffic between endpoints across untrusted networks
It assigns IP addresses to devices that join the network
explain: NAC evaluates a device's posture, such as patch level and endpoint protection status, as it connects, and can quarantine devices that do not comply. Perimeter inspection is a firewall/IPS role, and address assignment is DHCP.

q: For which type of network is a two-tier (collapsed core) design most suitable?
options: A very large service provider backbone network
A network that needs separate core and distribution layers for very high scale
A data center containing thousands of server racks
A small to medium network that does not need separate core and distribution layers
explain: In a collapsed core design the core and distribution functions share one layer of switches. That is simpler and cheaper, and it fits small to medium networks; very large networks need the layers separated to scale.

q: IP phones at a site are failing to register with the call manager. What should the technician check?
options: Whether the handsets are receiving the correct time from the NTP server
Whether moving the phones onto the data VLAN resolves the registration failure
Whether DHCP option 150 and TFTP are delivering the configuration, and whether the network path to the call manager works
Whether Power over Ethernet can be disabled on the switch ports serving the phones
explain: A phone needs an IP address, its configuration from a TFTP server (pointed to by DHCP option 150 on Cisco phones), and a working path to the call manager before it can register.

q: A network device loses its clock settings every time it reboots after a power loss. What is the most likely cause?
options: A failed internal real-time clock or backup battery
An NTP server configured with the wrong time zone
Incorrect daylight saving time rules in the device firmware
A switch port negotiating a half-duplex connection
explain: A dead internal clock/backup battery means the device cannot keep time while powered off, so the clock resets at every reboot. Time zone or NTP problems would cause a consistent offset, not a total loss of timekeeping.

q: What is the purpose of a cable lock on a portable network device?
options: To encrypt the data stored on the device
To prevent the device from joining unauthorized networks
To ground the device against electrostatic discharge
To deter opportunistic theft by physically securing the device
explain: A cable lock physically tethers a device so it cannot be casually carried away. It deters opportunistic theft but will not stop a determined thief, so it complements, rather than replaces, logical controls.

q: How does anomaly-based detection identify possible threats?
options: It compares traffic byte for byte against a database of known malware signatures
It flags activity that deviates from an established baseline of normal behavior
It blocks all traffic that has not been explicitly allowed by a rule
It requires an analyst to write a detection rule for every threat in advance
explain: Anomaly-based systems learn or are configured with what normal behavior looks like and alert on deviations, which can surface novel attacks. The trade-off is more tuning to control false alarms than with signature matching.

q: What is model-driven telemetry in network monitoring?
options: Polling devices at fixed intervals using SNMP requests
Sending syslog messages only when a fault occurs
Exporting performance counters manually whenever an engineer asks
Streaming structured metrics from devices to collectors in near real time
explain: Model-driven telemetry, using mechanisms such as gNMI over gRPC, has devices stream data to collectors on a subscription basis. That gives finer-grained, near-real-time data than periodic SNMP polling.

q: What does a wireless site survey determine?
options: The locations of wiring closets and backbone cable paths
The SSID names and password policies for the WLAN
Access point placement, channel selection, and transmit power settings
The number of users to assign to each VLAN
explain: A site survey, predictive or on-site, establishes where APs should go and which channels and power levels to use so coverage is adequate without excessive interference.

q: Which protocol and port does a full DNS zone transfer (AXFR) use?
options: TCP port 53
TCP port 80
UDP port 67
UDP port 53
explain: A full zone transfer moves a large amount of data and needs reliable delivery, so AXFR uses TCP port 53. Ordinary DNS queries normally use UDP port 53.

q: A backup WAN link is much slower than the primary link. What should the engineer address in the failover design?
options: Disable QoS so all traffic receives equal priority during failover
Apply QoS and traffic policies suited to the backup link's lower capacity
Increase the MTU on the primary link before failover occurs
Move LAN clients to static addressing for the duration of the outage
explain: When traffic fails over to a slower link, the policies tuned for the primary link no longer fit. Traffic must be prioritized and shaped for the reduced bandwidth so critical applications survive the failover.

q: Why are OSPF areas used in a large network?
options: To divide a single network into separate autonomous systems
To calculate interface costs automatically from link speed
To group routers according to their administrative security policies
To limit link-state flooding and the size of each router's link-state database, improving scalability
explain: Areas confine link-state advertisements to a smaller scope and let area border routers summarize routes into the backbone, area 0. That keeps LSDBs and SPF calculations manageable as the network grows.

q: How often should a backup generator typically be exercised under load?
options: Once a year, during the annual maintenance visit
Monthly, under load
Only after an actual power outage has occurred
Every five years, when the fuel supply is replaced
explain: Generators that are never run under load tend to fail when they are actually needed. Regular load testing, commonly monthly for emergency systems, verifies starting, transfer, and operation under real demand.

q: Which service uses TCP port 25 by default?
options: HTTP
POP3
SMTP
IMAP
explain: SMTP transfers mail between servers on TCP port 25; message submission commonly uses port 587. POP3 (110) and IMAP (143) are mailbox retrieval protocols, and HTTP uses port 80.

q: What do DHCP options 66 and 150 provide to clients?
options: The IP addresses of the DNS servers clients should use
The IP address of the default gateway for the subnet
The addresses of TFTP provisioning servers for devices such as IP phones
The IP addresses of the NTP servers clients should use
explain: Options 66 and 150 point clients, most commonly IP phones, at TFTP servers that hold their configuration and firmware. DNS is option 6, the gateway is option 3, and NTP is option 42.

q: Why should rollback criteria be defined before a change is implemented?
options: To guarantee that the change will never need to be reversed
To identify who will approve the change after it is implemented
To establish in advance the conditions that will trigger reverting the change
To document the final configuration after a successful change
explain: Agreeing the triggers beforehand, such as failed checks or a time limit, makes the back-out decision fast and objective when a change goes wrong, instead of being debated mid-incident.

q: At which layer of the OSI model do routers primarily operate?
options: Layer 2, the Data Link layer
Layer 1, the Physical layer
Layer 3, the Network layer
Layer 7, the Application layer
explain: Routers make forwarding decisions using logical IP addresses, which is Layer 3, Network layer, work. Switches forward on MAC addresses at Layer 2.

q: How can vendor documentation help when troubleshooting a device problem?
options: It directs the engineer to third-party forums for unofficial workarounds
It provides pricing and licensing details for replacement parts
It identifies the sales contacts for a support contract renewal
It provides command references and field notices that describe the device's exact behavior
explain: Official command references, release notes, and field notices state precisely how a device behaves, including known defects. That is more reliable for exact behavior than forum posts or guesswork.

q: Compared with the 2.4 GHz band, what does the 5 GHz Wi-Fi band offer?
options: Higher throughput and more channels, but shorter range
Lower throughput and fewer channels, but longer range
The same range with much better penetration through walls
Lower throughput with less congestion in all environments
explain: The 5 GHz band provides more non-overlapping channels and higher data rates, and is generally less congested. The trade-off is shorter range and weaker wall penetration than 2.4 GHz.

q: Why is labeling cables and ports important while troubleshooting?
options: It identifies which cables are permitted to carry Power over Ethernet
It satisfies the formatting requirements of the change ticket
It prevents new mistakes, such as disconnecting the wrong link, and makes changes traceable
It certifies that a cable has passed its performance tests
explain: Under pressure it is easy to unplug or move the wrong connection. Labeling as you go keeps every change identifiable and reversible, so troubleshooting does not create a second fault.

q: An IPS alert has been investigated and confirmed to be a false positive. What should the analyst do next?
options: Tune the signature or create a narrowly scoped exception for the verified benign traffic
Disable the IPS sensor until the vendor releases an update
Block the source address permanently at the perimeter firewall
Delete the logs relating to the alert from the SIEM
explain: Once the traffic is verified as benign, the signature is tuned or excepted for that specific case so the alert stops recurring. Disabling the sensor or blocking legitimate traffic would create bigger problems than the false alarm.

q: Which activities are part of cryptographic key management?
options: Labeling cables, configuring port security, and controlling rack access
Resetting user passwords and unlocking directory accounts
Securely generating, storing, rotating, and recovering or escrowing keys
Hashing user passwords and enforcing password complexity rules
explain: Key management covers the whole key lifecycle: generation, storage, distribution, rotation, and recovery or escrow. Losing control of keys can mean losing the data they protect, so the lifecycle has to be planned.

q: What does signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) measure?
options: The strength of the transmitted signal on its own
The distance a signal can travel before it attenuates
The maximum channel width available to a radio
The strength of the desired signal relative to the background noise floor
explain: SNR compares the wanted signal with the noise present in the environment. A higher SNR means a cleaner signal, which lets radios use faster modulation schemes and achieve higher data rates.

q: What is a captive portal?
options: A wireless network that encrypts all guest traffic by default
An authentication server that validates 802.1X credentials
A web page that requires a login or acceptance of terms before network access is granted
A firewall rule set that blocks access to social media sites
explain: A captive portal intercepts a new user's session and presents a sign-in or acceptable-use page before allowing access. It suits guest onboarding but is not encryption and is not a substitute for WPA or 802.1X security.

q: Which set of features makes up IPv6 first-hop security?
options: DHCP snooping, Dynamic ARP Inspection, and port security
NAT64, DNS64, and 464XLAT translation
RA Guard, DHCPv6 Guard, and IPv6 Source Guard
HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP gateway redundancy
explain: IPv6 first-hop security protects the local link with features such as RA Guard (blocking rogue router advertisements), DHCPv6 Guard/snooping, and source guard. The first option is the equivalent IPv4 suite, and HSRP/VRRP are redundancy protocols, not security controls.

q: What is delay skew in a twisted-pair copper cable?
options: The difference in arrival time between signals traveling on different wire pairs
The difference between the cable's measured length and its labeled length
The delay added while packets wait in a congested switch buffer
The total time a signal takes to travel from one end of the cable to the other
explain: Delay skew is the spread in propagation time between the pairs in one cable. If one pair delivers its signal much later than the others, high-speed signaling that recombines the pairs fails, and the cable must be replaced.

q: How is a duplicate IP address on a network commonly detected?
options: DNS returns two different names for the same host
Traceroute shows the same hop appearing twice in the path
ARP conflicts, duplicate-address warnings from operating systems, and inconsistent ARP tables
Ping replies from the address arrive with steadily increasing TTL values
explain: Two devices claiming one address produce ARP conflicts and OS duplicate-address warnings, and the ARP table entry flips between two MAC addresses. Switch MAC tables then help locate the offending device.

q: Why should a network team keep performance baselines?
options: To replace real-time monitoring with historical reports
To give auditors evidence of past performance only
To set maximum thresholds that network traffic must never exceed
To compare current behavior against known-normal performance and distinguish faults from normal variation
explain: A baseline records what healthy performance, traffic, and captures look like. Without that reference, it is hard to tell whether a current reading is a fault or just the network's normal pattern.

q: What should a complete set of network diagrams show?
options: Both the physical layout and the logical topology of the network
Only IP addressing and subnet details for each segment
Only rack elevations and device models
Only the WAN carrier circuits and their identifiers
explain: Physical diagrams show where equipment and cabling actually are, while logical diagrams show how traffic and addressing fit together. Troubleshooting and planning need both views.

q: Which set of items belongs in a network troubleshooting field toolkit?
options: A cable tester, a laptop, a console cable, and spare optics/transceivers
A smartphone and a printed contact list only
Cloud-based software tools with no physical test equipment
Replacement switches and routers only
explain: A ready go-bag with test and access basics, such as a cable tester, laptop, console cable, and spare transceivers, lets an engineer start work on site immediately instead of waiting for equipment to arrive.

q: What does IGMP snooping do on a Layer 2 switch?
options: It routes multicast traffic between different VLANs
It translates multicast group addresses into unicast addresses
It forwards multicast traffic only to the ports with interested receivers
It blocks all multicast traffic on the switch by default
explain: By listening to IGMP join and leave messages, the switch learns which ports have receivers for each group and sends multicast only there. Without snooping, multicast is flooded like broadcast traffic.

q: What is the purpose of certificate revocation mechanisms such as CRLs and OCSP?
options: To issue new certificates to servers that request them
To indicate that a compromised or no longer trusted certificate has been revoked before it expires
To extend the expiration date of a certificate that is still valid
To encrypt application traffic using the certificate's public key
explain: Revocation tells clients not to trust a certificate anymore, for example after its private key is compromised. CRLs publish lists of revoked certificates, and OCSP lets a client check a certificate's status directly.

q: Why should an engineer verify the MD5 or SHA hash of a firmware image before an upgrade?
options: To encrypt the image before it is installed on the device
To confirm the image is intact and matches the vendor-published version
To compress the image so that it fits in the device's flash memory
To convert the image so it can run on a different hardware model
explain: Comparing the downloaded image's hash with the vendor's published value proves the file was not corrupted or tampered with in transit. Installing a damaged image can fail the upgrade or leave the device unbootable.

q: Legitimate traffic is being blocked by a firewall. What should the engineer check first?
options: Whether the firewall has enough throughput capacity for the traffic volume
The rule order, rule hit counts, and implicit deny log entries, to find the rule blocking the traffic
Whether the DNS records for the destination point to its public address
Whether replacing the firewall with a newer model resolves the block
explain: Firewalls act on the first matching rule and deny anything unmatched, so the blocking entry is found by reviewing rule order and the hits logged against deny rules, including the implicit deny at the end.

q: Which ports does RADIUS use by default for authentication and accounting?
options: TCP port 22 for authentication and TCP port 23 for accounting
TCP port 443 for authentication and TCP port 8443 for accounting
UDP port 53 for authentication and UDP port 5353 for accounting
UDP port 1812 for authentication and UDP port 1813 for accounting
explain: RADIUS authentication runs on UDP 1812 and accounting on UDP 1813. RADIUS provides the back end for 802.1X, WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise, and VPN user authentication.

q: Which set of symptoms indicates that a network device is overheating?
options: Thermal throttling, intermittent errors, and unexpected shutdowns
Slow DNS resolution, intermittent DHCP failures, and address conflicts
Frequent link flaps, duplex errors, and spanning-tree reconvergence
Certificate errors, clock drift, and failed NTP synchronization
explain: Overheated equipment protects itself by throttling, generates errors, and may shut down entirely. The checks are internal temperatures, fan operation, and blocked airflow in the rack or closet.

q: What does API-driven monitoring enable?
options: Manual polling of each device by a technician using a console session
Replacement of all monitoring data with syslog messages from devices
Programmatic integration of monitoring data with other tools, such as ticketing, CMDB, and automation systems
Collection of monitoring data from devices with no network connectivity
explain: Monitoring platforms with APIs can feed their data directly into ticketing, CMDB, and automation workflows and accept data from other tools. That integration removes manual copying between systems.

q: What is the purpose of the aging time on a switch's MAC address table?
options: It removes stale entries after a period of inactivity, commonly about 300 seconds by default
It sets how long a port stays in the spanning-tree listening state
It sets the interval at which hosts refresh their ARP caches
It controls how often the switch floods frames for known unicast addresses
explain: Devices move and power off, so switches age out MAC entries that have gone quiet, commonly after about 300 seconds by default, though the value is configurable. That keeps the table accurate and leaves room for active devices.

q: A host has an incorrect ARP entry as a result of ARP poisoning. What is the best remediation?
options: Wait for the DHCP lease to renew so the host receives a corrected entry
Clear the affected ARP entries and enable Dynamic ARP Inspection on the switch
Replace the network cables between the affected hosts
Assign the affected host a new hostname and rejoin it to the domain
explain: Clearing the cache removes the poisoned entry immediately, and Dynamic ARP Inspection prevents a recurrence by validating ARP messages against the DHCP snooping binding table.

q: Why would an engineer implement a separate voice VLAN for IP phones?
options: To separate VoIP traffic from data traffic so it can be prioritized and managed with its own policies
To encrypt all voice calls by default as they cross the LAN
To give the phones IP addresses without using DHCP
To increase the total bandwidth available on the access switch uplink
explain: A voice VLAN keeps phone traffic apart from PC data traffic, typically with the phone tagging voice frames and passing data through untagged. That separation lets QoS protect call quality from data bursts.

q: How does keeping a known-good baseline configuration for each device role help during recovery?
options: It provides a trusted configuration that can be compared against or restored after a failure or bad change
It records real-time performance metrics used for capacity planning
It lists the approved vendors for purchasing replacement hardware
It documents the physical rack layout for the installation team
explain: Archived golden configurations let you diff a suspect device against a known-good state or restore that state outright. That is much faster and safer than rebuilding a configuration from memory during an outage.

q: How does anycast deliver traffic for a service such as DNS?
options: The service address is broadcast to all clients on the local subnet
Clients are assigned to servers manually in round-robin order
The same IP address is announced from multiple locations, and routing sends each client to the topologically nearest instance
Each server uses a unique address, and clients work through a list in order until one answers
explain: With anycast, many instances share one address and all announce it; the routing system carries each request to the best-path instance. This gives proximity and resilience for services such as DNS and CDNs.

q: A traceroute repeatedly cycles through the same set of hops and reports TTL-expired messages. What does this indicate?
options: The DNS resolver is returning stale records for the destination
A duplex mismatch exists on the local access link
The destination host is silently discarding all ICMP traffic
A routing loop exists on the path to the destination
explain: In a routing loop, packets pass between the same routers until their TTL reaches zero, and each router reports time exceeded. The fix is in the routing tables or protocol configuration creating the loop.

q: Why do automated change workflows perform pre-checks and post-checks?
options: To create an additional change ticket for every device touched
To bypass the need for formal approval of the change
To increase deployment speed even when the results are unknown
To record the starting state and verify that the change produced the intended result
explain: Pre-checks capture the state before the change and post-checks test the state afterward, so automation can confirm success or trigger a rollback. That closes the verification loop on every automated change.

q: A network engineer subnets 192.168.1.0/24 into /26 subnets. How many subnets and usable hosts per subnet result?
options: 16 subnets with 14 usable hosts each
4 subnets with 62 usable hosts each
8 subnets with 30 usable hosts each
2 subnets with 126 usable hosts each
explain: Moving from /24 to /26 borrows 2 bits, giving 2^2 = 4 subnets. Each /26 leaves 6 host bits, so 2^6 - 2 = 62 usable host addresses per subnet.

q: How is the DNS root server system organized?
options: As 13 logical server clusters, identified by letters, operated at locations worldwide
As a single physical server located in one country
As one root server operated by each ISP for its own customers
As 13 individual physical servers with no anycast distribution
explain: There are 13 named root server identities, a through m, but each is served by many anycast instances around the world. That design gives the root zone global reach and resilience.

q: How is network traffic typically monitored in a cloud environment, where physical taps are unavailable?
options: By configuring SPAN sessions on the provider's physical switches
By relying on end users to report any traffic problems they notice
By using flow logs and the provider's native monitoring tools and agents
By installing a hardware tap on each virtual link between instances
explain: Cloud platforms replace physical taps and SPAN ports with VPC flow logs, native monitoring services, and in-instance agents. Those sources provide the visibility needed for troubleshooting and security monitoring.

q: Where does queueing delay occur in a network?
options: In long fiber runs, because of the speed of light in glass
At the endpoints, while applications process the received data
At congested router or switch interfaces, while packets wait in buffers
During the DNS lookup that takes place before a connection opens
explain: Queueing delay is the time packets spend waiting in an output buffer when an interface cannot forward them as fast as they arrive. Congested interfaces are therefore a major source of latency and jitter.

q: What do incident escalation policies define?
options: When an issue should be escalated and to whom it should be escalated
Which manager must personally perform all troubleshooting tasks
Which paging vendor the organization must purchase its service from
How long every incident must remain open before it may be closed
explain: Escalation policies set the tiers, time frames, and hand-off points for raising an issue to more senior staff or other teams. Clear rules prevent both delayed escalation and unnecessary escalation.

q: Why should disruptive network tests be performed during a maintenance window?
options: To keep the results of the tests hidden from users and management
To allow the tests to run without logging or formal approval
To increase the chance that faults will occur during business hours
To limit the impact on users if the testing disrupts service
explain: Intrusive diagnostics can drop links or overload devices, so they belong in an approved maintenance window when user impact is lowest and stakeholders expect possible disruption.

q: What are STIX and TAXII used for in threat intelligence?
options: To encrypt threat intelligence feeds between organizations
To convert malware samples into firewall signatures automatically
To exchange threat indicators between systems in a standard, machine-readable way
To store firewall logs in a SIEM using a common event schema
explain: STIX provides the standard language for describing threat indicators and relationships, and TAXII is the transport for exchanging them. Together they let security platforms share intelligence automatically, machine to machine.

q: What is a split DNS configuration?
options: A single DNS server that returns two addresses for every name for load balancing
A configuration in which internal and external clients receive different answers for the same names
A zone split so that the primary and secondary servers each hold half of the records
A zone duplicated onto two servers purely for redundancy
explain: Split DNS (split-horizon views) serves different answers depending on where the query comes from: internal clients get private addresses for a name while external clients get its public address.

q: How can a technician diagnose a suspected packet fragmentation or path MTU problem?
options: By querying DNS for the MTU record of the destination server
By inspecting the ARP cache for oversized address entries
By sending ping sweeps with the Don't Fragment bit set while varying the packet size
By running a traceroute and counting the hops to the destination
explain: Sending DF-bit pings at decreasing sizes finds the largest packet that crosses the path intact, which reveals the real path MTU. Failures at a specific size pinpoint where oversized packets are being dropped.

q: Which metrics are most important when monitoring real-time video traffic quality?
options: Bitrate, packet loss, and jitter
The number of user accounts and failed login attempts
DNS query counts and resolver cache hit ratio
Switch port speed and duplex status only
explain: Video quality depends on sustained bitrate and is visibly degraded by packet loss and jitter, which cause freezing and artifacts. Monitoring only whether a service is up misses those quality problems.

q: How do webhook-based alerts deliver monitoring events to other systems?
options: They push event data immediately to a receiving URL used by chat, ticketing, or automation tools
They require a technician to poll the monitoring server every few minutes for new events
They send alerts only as scheduled email summaries
They store alerts on the monitored device until it is next rebooted
explain: A webhook sends an HTTP message to a configured URL the moment an event occurs, so tools such as chat platforms, paging services, and SOAR playbooks can act on the alert right away instead of waiting to poll.

q: Why is accurate time synchronization across all network devices critical for security investigations?
options: Correlating log timestamps accurately across different devices
Calculating the fastest switching path for Ethernet frames
Assigning IP addresses automatically to newly connected hosts
Encrypting management traffic between switches and routers
explain: Network Time Protocol (NTP) keeps device clocks aligned, so log entries from firewalls, servers, and routers can be placed in the correct order during an investigation. If clocks drift, timestamps no longer line up and the sequence of events becomes unreliable.

q: According to the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology, what should a technician do immediately after identifying the problem?
options: Document the findings and close the support ticket
Establish a theory of probable cause
Implement a solution and test its functionality
Escalate the issue to the equipment vendor
explain: The methodology orders the steps as identify the problem, then establish a theory of probable cause, then test that theory. Jumping straight to a fix risks random changes that can make an outage worse.

q: An interface shows a rising count of input errors and overruns, but no CRC errors. What is the most likely cause?
options: A duplex mismatch corrupting frames on the link
Damaged cabling causing corrupted frames to arrive
Excessive broadcast traffic saturating the local VLAN
Interface overruns caused by congestion exceeding the buffer capacity
explain: Overrun and ignored counters mean frames arrived faster than the interface could process them and were dropped from full buffers. CRC errors would point instead to cabling or duplex problems, which corrupt frames rather than overflow buffers.

q: What is the purpose of an ephemeral port on a client device?
options: To listen permanently for incoming service requests
To serve as a temporary source port for outbound sessions
To identify the VLAN membership of a switch port
To provide a well-known port number for a server application
explain: When a client opens a connection, it selects a temporary ephemeral port, typically from 49152 to 65535, as its source port. Well-known ports are used on the server side for listening, not on the client side.

q: Users report high latency only when accessing one specific remote destination, while other destinations respond normally. Which tool should be used first to locate the delay?
options: Traceroute to identify the slow hop along the path
Nslookup to verify the destination DNS record
A cable tester to check the local patch cable
A spectrum analyzer to check for wireless interference
explain: Traceroute reports the round-trip time to each hop along the path, which reveals where latency is introduced for that one destination. DNS or cabling faults would affect name resolution or all traffic, not a single remote path.

q: What should an organization do when a vendor announces end-of-life (EOL) for a network device it relies on?
options: Begin refresh planning and budgeting for a replacement
Remove the device from service immediately, regardless of impact
Wait until the device fails completely before planning a replacement
Purchase additional units of the same EOL model as spares
explain: EOL means the vendor will stop providing support, parts, and security updates, so refresh planning should start as soon as the announcement arrives. Waiting for a failure leaves the network running unsupported equipment with no replacement ready.

q: What is the role of a DNS forwarder on an internal DNS server?
options: To host the authoritative zone records for a domain
To block all external DNS queries from internal clients
To cache external answers without contacting any other server
To send unresolved external queries to an upstream DNS server
explain: A forwarder passes queries it cannot answer locally to an upstream server, such as an ISP or public resolver, and returns the result to the client. Authoritative servers host zone records themselves instead of forwarding them.

q: Which statement correctly describes a proxy ARP entry?
options: It is manually configured so a router answers ARP requests on behalf of another host
It is learned dynamically from DNS zone transfer records
It is created automatically by DHCP for every address lease
It is a routing table entry that points to a remote network
explain: With proxy ARP, a router is configured to reply to ARP requests for another host's IP address using its own MAC address. It is a special-case configuration, unlike normal ARP entries that hosts learn dynamically from replies.

q: How does Kerberos provide authentication on a network?
options: By using one shared pre-shared key for every service
By sending user passwords across the network in clear text
By relying solely on digital certificates for all authentication
By issuing tickets through a Key Distribution Center on port 88
explain: Kerberos uses a Key Distribution Center (KDC) on port 88 to issue time-limited tickets that clients present to services, so passwords are not sent repeatedly. Because tickets are time-based, Kerberos also requires clocks to be synchronized.

q: Which observation most strongly indicates a broadcast storm on a switched network?
options: Low interface utilization with only occasional broadcast frames
Near 100 percent utilization with all interfaces flooding broadcast traffic
A single host failing to obtain an address from DHCP
High CPU utilization on one workstation with normal switch traffic
explain: A switching loop causes broadcast frames to be forwarded endlessly and multiplied, driving utilization toward 100 percent on many interfaces at once. Spanning Tree and storm control are used to prevent and contain this condition.

q: What is a primary goal of tuning an intrusion prevention system (IPS)?
options: To enable every available signature regardless of relevance
To block all traffic that matches any signature, without exception
To replace the need for firewall rules on the network perimeter
To reduce false positives while keeping detection effective
explain: An untuned IPS generates false positives that can block legitimate traffic and overwhelm analysts with noise. Tuning baselines the environment and enables the relevant signatures so real attacks are still caught with fewer false alarms.

q: In routing, what is a metric?
options: A physical cable category used to connect two routers
A value a routing protocol calculates to select the best path
A well-known port number assigned to a routing protocol
An IP address that identifies a directly connected neighbor
explain: A metric is the cost value a protocol assigns to a route, such as hop count in RIP or cost based on bandwidth in OSPF. When several routes to the same destination exist within one protocol, the lowest metric wins.

q: Under which condition does certificate pinning most often cause an application to fail?
options: When TLS inspection replaces the server certificate with a proxy certificate
When DNS resolves the server name to its correct IP address
When a standard TLS session is established without any interception
When the application connects to a server over plain HTTP
explain: A pinned application expects a specific certificate or public key for the server and refuses any other. TLS inspection presents the proxy's certificate instead, so the pin check fails and the connection is rejected unless the application is bypassed.

q: What metric does the Routing Information Protocol (RIP) use to select the best path?
options: Hop count, with a maximum of 15 usable hops
Available bandwidth across the slowest link in the path
The configured maximum transmission unit of each interface
Cumulative delay measured along the path in microseconds
explain: RIP counts router hops and prefers the route with the fewest, treating 16 hops as unreachable. That 15-hop ceiling is why RIP is limited to relatively small networks, unlike OSPF which uses a bandwidth-based cost.

q: Why should BGP sessions with external peers be continuously monitored?
options: To alert administrators when a BGP peer flaps or goes down
To assign private IP addresses to newly configured BGP neighbors
