As the only source for critical configurations
As proof that a device is faulty
As a supplement to vendor documentation with real-world cases
explain: Community forums and labs surface real-world edge cases that official documents may miss. They work best as a supplement to vendor documentation, not a replacement for it.

q: IPv6 unique local addresses (ULA) fall within which prefix?
explain: fc00::/7 is the unique local range, the IPv6 equivalent of IPv4's private RFC 1918 space. fe80::/10 is link-local, which is a different, non-routable scope.

q: A firewall is blocking a site-to-site VPN. Which traffic must the firewall allow?
options: Only TCP port 443 for HTTPS
UDP 500, UDP 4500, and ESP
Only UDP port 53 for DNS
Only ICMP echo requests
explain: IPsec needs IKE on UDP 500, NAT traversal on UDP 4500, and the ESP protocol itself. If the edge ACL blocks any of these, the tunnel cannot come up.

q: Asset refresh cycles in a lifecycle plan should ensure which of the following?
options: Equipment is kept until it fails completely
Gear is replaced before it reaches end of life or end of support
Only end-user PCs are ever replaced
Devices are refreshed only after a security incident
explain: Refresh planning replaces gear before support ends, typically on a multi-year cycle. Unsupported equipment is a security and reliability risk because it no longer receives fixes.

q: What is the main security risk of split tunneling on a VPN client?
options: It always makes the VPN connection too slow to use
It prevents the remote user from reaching the Internet
The remote host can expose the corporate LAN to untrusted networks
It forces the use of certificate authentication
explain: With split tunneling, the remote host reaches the Internet and the corporate LAN at the same time, so it can become a bridge that bypasses inspection controls. The convenience must be weighed against that exposure.

q: In device lifecycle terms, Day 0, Day 1, and Day 2 refer to which phases?
options: The same tasks repeated on three consecutive days
Provisioning, initial configuration, and ongoing operation
A mandatory three-day installation window
Maintenance phases that apply only to servers
explain: Day 0 is provisioning, Day 1 is initial configuration and deployment, and Day 2 covers ongoing operations and management. Structuring automation around these phases keeps lifecycle tasks organized.

q: A PC can ping its default gateway but cannot reach the Internet. What should be checked next?
options: The VLAN assigned to the PC's switchport
The PC's own Ethernet cable
Routing, NAT, firewall rules, and the ISP link
The MAC address table on the local switch
explain: Reaching the gateway proves the local network path works, so the fault lies upstream. Check the edge routing, NAT, firewall policy, and the provider link next.

q: Which characteristic defines a chassis switch?
options: A fixed number of ports with no expansion options
A design intended only for home networks
An inability to accept supervisor modules
Modular slots that allow expansion with line cards
explain: A chassis switch has slots that accept line cards and supervisor modules, so capacity can grow by adding cards. This modular design suits campus and core deployments that need to scale.

q: EIRP for a wireless transmitter is calculated as which of the following?
options: Receiver sensitivity minus the noise floor
Antenna gain with no other factors
Cable length multiplied by transmitter power
Transmitter power plus antenna gain minus losses
explain: EIRP (effective isotropic radiated power) equals transmit power plus antenna gain minus cable and connector losses. Regulators cap EIRP, so installations must stay within the legal limit.

q: Which pair describes the common deployment modes of a web application firewall?
options: Active-active or active-passive clustering
Inline blocking or monitor-only detection
Cloud-hosted or appliance-based hosting
Signature-based or anomaly-based detection
explain: A WAF can run inline and actively block malicious requests, or in monitor-only mode that alerts without blocking. Teams often tune rules in monitor mode first, then switch to blocking.

q: What is the goal of root cause analysis after an incident?
options: To assign blame to the person on call
To close the ticket as quickly as possible
To document the outage without making changes
To identify the underlying cause and apply a systemic fix
explain: Root cause analysis looks past the immediate symptom to the underlying cause, so the fix prevents recurrence. Done well, it turns an outage into a permanent improvement.

q: Security baselines such as CIS benchmarks are used to do what?
options: Increase the forwarding speed of devices
Harden devices consistently using standard secure settings
Replace the vendor's own documentation
Disable security controls that slow traffic
explain: CIS and NIST benchmarks give a standard set of hardening settings so devices are configured securely and consistently. Auditing against the baseline catches configuration drift.

q: A MAC address is best described as which of the following?
options: A 48-bit hardware address used at Layer 2
A 128-bit address assigned by a DHCP server
A variable-length name resolved by DNS
A 32-bit logical address used at Layer 3
explain: A MAC address is a 48-bit hardware identifier used for frame delivery on the local network at Layer 2. The 32-bit logical address in the distractors describes IPv4.

q: What is the typical order of name resolution on a client?
options: DNS server first, then cache, then hosts file
Hosts file first, then DNS server, then cache
LLMNR first, then the DNS server, then the cache
Cache first, then hosts file, then DNS server
explain: Clients first check their local resolver cache, then the hosts file, and only then query the configured DNS server. This order avoids unnecessary DNS traffic for names already resolved.

q: The Physical layer (Layer 1) of the OSI model is responsible for what?
options: Managing sessions between two hosts
Encrypting data for the Application layer
Routing packets between different networks
Transmitting raw bits over cabling and signaling
explain: Layer 1 moves raw bits over physical media and defines cables, connectors, and signaling. Hubs and repeaters operate at this layer.

q: A screened subnet (DMZ) differs from a plain VLAN because it does what?
options: Forwards traffic faster than a VLAN
Operates without any switch at all
Connects zones over a wireless link
Adds firewall policy controlling traffic between trust zones
explain: A VLAN alone only segments traffic, while a screened subnet pairs segmentation with firewall rules between zones of different trust. That policy enforcement is what makes it a DMZ.

q: Administrative distance is used to measure what about a route?
options: How trustworthy the route's source is
The physical length of the cable to the next hop
The maximum speed of the outgoing link
The strength of the password protecting the route
explain: Administrative distance ranks how trustworthy a route source is, and the lower value wins. For example, a static route (1) beats OSPF (110), which beats RIP (120).

q: Exceeding the minimum bend radius of a fiber cable can cause what?
options: A stronger received optical signal
Signal loss and possible damage to the fiber
Faster transmission over the link
Automatic rerouting of traffic to a spare strand
explain: Sharp bends let light escape the core (macrobending), which causes signal loss and can permanently damage the fiber. Always respect the cable's minimum bend radius.

q: An SSID is which of the following?
options: The password used to join a wireless network
The MAC address of an access point
The network name advertised by access points
The encryption standard used by the network
explain: The SSID is simply the name that identifies a wireless network and is broadcast by its access points. Hiding the SSID is not real security, since it can still be discovered.

q: Rolling back a recent change during troubleshooting is useful because it can do what?
options: Hide the true cause of the problem
Avoid the need to document the incident
Prevent the change from ever being reapplied later
Confirm whether that change caused the problem
explain: If the problem disappears when a change is reverted, that change caused it. Rollback is a valid diagnostic step as well as a recovery step.

q: IEEE 802.3 defines which technology?
options: Token Ring networks
Wired Ethernet
Wi-Fi wireless LANs
Bluetooth personal area networks
explain: 802.3 is the Ethernet standard. By contrast, 802.11 defines Wi-Fi, 802.1Q defines VLAN tagging, and 802.1X defines port-based authentication.

q: Keeping spare cables and SFP modules on hand helps troubleshooting because they allow what?
options: Cheaper installations of new equipment
Elimination of testing during an outage
Prevention of all hardware failures
Fast substitution tests to isolate a faulty component
explain: Swapping in a known-good cable or SFP is one of the fastest ways to tell whether a component is faulty. Substitution removes guesswork from hardware diagnosis.

q: A/B testing a network change involves which approach?
options: Applying the change to all users at the same time
Evaluating only the old configuration after rollout
Applying the change only to the newest hardware first
Comparing behavior between subsets running different versions
explain: A/B testing pilots a change on a subset and compares its behavior with the control group. This validates the change before a wide rollout.

q: Extended ACLs should generally be placed in which location?
options: Close to the source of the traffic
Close to the destination of the traffic
Only on the end hosts themselves
On the router farthest from the traffic
explain: Extended ACLs filter on detailed criteria, so placing them near the source drops unwanted traffic early and saves bandwidth. Standard ACLs, which filter only on source address, go near the destination instead.

q: Bufferbloat is best described as which of the following?
options: A buffering fault that occurs only on WAN links
A type of buffering that improves latency
Excessive buffering that causes large latency spikes
A memory error inside a switch
explain: Bufferbloat happens when oversized buffers hold packets too long, inflating latency for interactive traffic. Smart queue management such as FQ-CoDel keeps buffers from filling this way.

q: Document classification labels serve which purpose?
options: They visibly guide handlers on how the document must be protected
They set the retention period after which documents are destroyed
They mark the document as approved for public release
They identify only the document's author
explain: Classification markings tell anyone handling a document what protection it requires, such as storage and sharing limits. The visible label keeps those duties in front of the handler.

q: OSPF calculates the cost of a route primarily based on what?
options: Bandwidth, using a reference bandwidth (100 Mbps by default)
The configured subnet mask of each interface
Delay as the only metric
The number of hops to the destination
explain: OSPF cost equals the reference bandwidth divided by the interface bandwidth, so faster links get lower, preferred costs. The default reference bandwidth is 100 Mbps, though it can be raised for gigabit and faster links.

q: The active and passive modes of LACP are used to do what?
options: Negotiate the formation of a link aggregation bundle
Create a static bundle with no negotiation at all
Select channels for a wireless network
Assign IP addresses to bundled interfaces
explain: LACP active and passive modes negotiate the aggregated link, and at least one side must be active for the bundle to form. A static 'on/on' configuration does not negotiate.

q: In the client-server model, a server's role is to do what?
options: Provide services and resources to clients
Request services from clients only
Route packets between networks only
Store backup copies while staying offline
explain: A server hosts applications, files, and services that clients consume, such as web, email, or file services. Clients initiate the requests; servers respond to them.

q: An autonomous system (AS) is best defined as which of the following?
options: A single VLAN inside one switch
A network or group of networks under one administration
A single router in a provider network
A single host connected to the Internet
explain: An autonomous system is a collection of networks run under one administration with a common routing policy, identified by an ASN. BGP exchanges routes between these systems.

q: An oversubscription ratio compares which two quantities?
options: Power input to power output of a switch
The number of routers to the number of switches
Total downlink capacity to the available uplink capacity
The cost of the uplinks to the cost of the devices
explain: Oversubscription compares the combined access (downlink) capacity against the uplink capacity leaving that layer. A modest ratio such as 3:1 at access-to-distribution is common and acceptable.

q: Certificate-based VPN authentication compares with pre-shared keys how?
options: It is required only when the VPN carries IPv6 traffic
It is weaker because certificates can expire
It is stronger because identity is tied to an issued certificate
It is used only to secure websites
explain: Certificates tie a device or user identity to an issued, revocable credential instead of a shared secret everyone knows. Combined with MFA, this resists credential theft better than a pre-shared key.

q: TCP port 23 is used by which service?
options: FTP
Telnet
SSH
HTTP
explain: Port 23 is Telnet, which sends everything, including credentials, in cleartext. Use SSH on port 22 instead for secure remote administration.

q: Vulnerability scanning of network infrastructure helps an organization do what?
options: Find missing patches and misconfigurations
Apply only to end-user servers
Guarantee that no vulnerability will ever appear
Replace the patching process entirely
explain: Scanning switches, routers, and firewalls finds missing patches and insecure settings just as it does on servers. Infrastructure devices are assets and must be scanned like any other.

q: A QoS trust boundary defines which of the following?
options: Where DSCP or CoS markings from a device are accepted as trusted
The physical perimeter of the building
The set of VLANs permitted on a trunk
The location of the firewall rule base
explain: The trust boundary is the point where markings are accepted or rewritten. Trusted devices such as IP phones can have their markings honored, while untrusted PC traffic is remarked at the access edge.

q: A host is configured with the wrong default gateway. What is the most likely symptom?
options: Nothing on the network works at all
Only remote networks work, while local subnet traffic fails
Local subnet traffic works but remote networks fail
Only DNS lookups fail while routing works
explain: Hosts reach their own subnet directly, so local traffic still works with a wrong gateway. Anything off-subnet must go through the gateway, so remote access fails.

q: Why is stale monitoring data a problem?
options: It can mislead decisions, so the poller's health should be checked
It encrypts device data so only current values can be read
It is useful only for long-term history reports
It removes the need for alerting thresholds
explain: Dashboards built on stale data look current but describe the past, which misleads troubleshooting. Verify that the monitoring poller itself is healthy and data is fresh before trusting it.

q: A wireless site survey should be repeated in which situation?
options: Every day as a routine task
Only on the same date each year
Never, once the network is installed
After major changes to the environment or layout
explain: New walls, neighboring networks, or changes in user density alter RF conditions, so a fresh survey is needed after major environmental changes. A survey from before the change no longer reflects reality.

q: What is the primary role of a core switch?
options: Connecting end-user PCs in a small office
Acting as the firewall at the network edge
Providing high-speed backbone forwarding between distribution blocks
Assigning IP addresses to client devices
explain: The core layer prioritizes fast, redundant forwarding of traffic between distribution blocks. It favors speed and resilience over the feature-rich policy work done at other layers.

q: Disabling IP directed broadcast on a router helps prevent which attack?
options: MAC flooding of a switch
Smurf attacks that use broadcast amplification
ARP spoofing on the local segment
Rogue DHCP servers on a VLAN
explain: Directed broadcasts can amplify a spoofed ping so every host on a subnet replies to the victim, which is a smurf attack. Modern routers disable directed broadcast by default, but legacy gear should be verified.

q: Which set lists tools commonly used for network automation?
options: Graphical interfaces only
Telnet and manual typing only
Vendor web consoles only
Ansible, Terraform, and Python with Netmiko
explain: Tools such as Ansible, Terraform, and Python libraries like Netmiko automate network changes so they are consistent, reviewable, and repeatable. Manual CLI work alone does not scale or audit well.

q: Firmware upgrades are staged (rolled out in phases) in order to do what?
options: Slow down the overall upgrade schedule
Upgrade every device at the same moment
Skip testing the new firmware entirely
Limit the blast radius if the new firmware causes problems
explain: Staging upgrades on a pilot group first limits how much of the network a bad image can affect. Keep rollback images ready before expanding the rollout.

q: Which sequence correctly describes the vulnerability management cycle?
options: Scan once and close the process
Remediate first, then discover the assets
Discover, assess, remediate, then verify
Assess, ignore, scan, and archive
explain: The cycle discovers assets and vulnerabilities, assesses their risk, remediates them, and then verifies with a rescan that the fix worked. Skipping verification leaves the loop open.

q: Priority levels P1 through P4 are used to do what?
options: Label the types of cables in a rack
Rank vendors by importance
Classify the sensitivity of documents
Set response urgency, with SLAs attached to each level
explain: Priority levels define how urgently an incident must be handled, from a P1 outage needing immediate response to a cosmetic P4. Response and resolution SLAs are attached to each level.

q: UDP port 123 is used by which service?
options: SNMP
NTP
DHCP
DNS
explain: UDP 123 is NTP, the Network Time Protocol used to synchronize clocks. Accurate time matters for logs, certificates, and authentication.

q: DNS aging and scavenging perform which function?
options: They never run without a full server restart
They require an administrator to delete each record manually
They delete entire DNS zones on a schedule
They clean up stale dynamic DNS records automatically
explain: Scavenging automatically removes outdated dynamic DNS records that clients registered but never cleaned up. This keeps the zone accurate and prevents stale entries from resolving to the wrong host.

q: An optical light meter is used to verify what on a fiber link?
options: The end-to-end latency of the link
The application throughput of the link
That received optical power is within the link budget
The maximum bandwidth the fiber can carry
explain: A light meter measures received optical power in dBm, which is compared against the link budget to confirm the signal is strong enough. It measures power, not speed or latency.

q: A dual-stack network or host is one that is doing what?
options: Running IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time
Running two separate IPv4 configurations
Using two network cables for redundancy
Using two default gateways for one protocol
explain: Dual-stack means a device runs both IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously during the transition between them. Each protocol operates with its own addressing on the same host.

q: An access point's transmit power should generally be set how?
options: Set 3 dB above the client's maximum on every AP
To the maximum setting at all times
Matched to the transmit capabilities of the client devices
To the minimum setting at all times
explain: If an AP transmits far more powerfully than clients can answer, the result is a one-way link where clients hear the AP but cannot be heard. Matching AP power to client capability keeps links two-way.

q: Performance testing after an upgrade is important in order to do what?
options: Confirm the vendor's claims without a baseline
Validate that the upgrade caused no performance regression
Replace the need for monitoring after the upgrade
Delay the return to production use
explain: Comparing post-upgrade performance against the pre-upgrade baseline proves the change helped and did not quietly degrade service. Without the comparison, a regression can go unnoticed.

q: Standard operating procedures (SOPs) are used to do what?
options: Let each technician improvise routine tasks
Replace all technician training
Apply only in factory environments
Document routine tasks so they are performed consistently
explain: SOPs record the approved steps for routine tasks so any technician performs them the same way. That consistency makes operations repeatable and auditable.

q: Scheduled jobs (such as kron on network devices) are used to do what?
options: Require tasks to be run manually
Apply only to Linux servers
Configure devices through an interactive session
Automate periodic tasks such as backups and reports
explain: On-device schedulers run commands automatically at set times, which suits recurring jobs like configuration backups and report generation. This removes reliance on someone remembering to run them.

q: One VPN peer is configured for IKEv1 and the other for IKEv2. What is the result?
options: The IKEv2 peer downgrades the session to IKEv1 during Phase 2
Negotiation fails until both peers use the same IKE version
The tunnel establishes with reduced encryption
Only Phase 2 of the tunnel fails
explain: IKEv1 and IKEv2 are not interchangeable during negotiation, so mismatched versions prevent the tunnel from forming. Standardize both peers on the same IKE version.

q: A toner and probe kit is used to do what?
options: Test the light levels in a fiber run
Trace and identify cable runs through walls
Measure the power output of a device
Clean dust from cable connectors
explain: A tone generator puts a signal on a cable and an inductive probe detects it along the run, identifying unlabeled cables. It traces copper cabling; it does not measure fiber light levels.

q: A privileged access workstation (PAW) is best described as which of the following?
options: A standard workstation for everyday user tasks
A workstation provided for guest access
A hardened device dedicated only to administrative tasks
A shared kiosk used by all staff
explain: A PAW is a hardened, dedicated machine used only for sensitive administrative work, separate from daily browsing and email. This isolation reduces the chance that a compromised everyday PC yields admin credentials.

q: A MOS score of 4.0 or higher indicates what about a voice call?
options: Good call quality
Poor call quality
That no calls were completed
That the voice test failed
explain: The Mean Opinion Score rates voice quality from 1 to 5, and 4.0 or above is considered good, near toll quality. Scores below about 3.6 are where users start noticing problems.

q: Unknown unicast flooding occurs when a switch does what?
options: Encrypts frames addressed to unknown hosts
Drops every frame for an unknown MAC address
Sends frames for an unknown destination MAC out all ports in the VLAN
Routes frames for unknown hosts to the default gateway
explain: If a switch has not learned a destination MAC, it floods the frame out all ports in the VLAN until the address is learned. Attackers can exploit this flooding to sniff traffic.

q: Syslog severity levels range across which values?
options: Letters A through Z
Numbers 1 through 5 only
Numbers 0 through 100
0 for emergency through 7 for debug
explain: Syslog severities run from 0 (emergency, most severe) to 7 (debug, least severe). Lower numbers always mean more serious events.

q: A Wi-Fi spectrum analyzer is most useful for identifying what?
options: Sources of non-Wi-Fi radio interference
Faults in a copper cable run
Light loss in a fiber link
The throughput of an application
explain: A spectrum analyzer shows raw RF energy, revealing non-Wi-Fi interferers like microwaves, wireless cameras, and jammers that a normal Wi-Fi scan cannot see. This makes it the right tool for unexplained wireless interference.

q: A load balancer distributes which of the following?
options: Cables among equipment racks
VLANs among access switches
IP addresses among routers
Incoming traffic across multiple servers
explain: A load balancer spreads incoming traffic across a pool of servers using algorithms such as round-robin or least connections. This provides both scale and failover if a server goes down.

q: A clean-desk policy helps an organization do what?
options: Ensure desks are sanitized between shifts
Make security policies optional for staff
Increase the storage of paper records at desks
Reduce the physical exposure of sensitive data
explain: Clean-desk rules require locking screens, shredding sensitive papers, and securing removable media. These basics reduce the chance that sensitive information is seen or taken from unattended desks.

q: An IPv6 link-local address always begins with which prefix?
explain: Link-local IPv6 addresses use fe80::/10 and are auto-configured for communication on a single link only. fc00::/7 is unique local, and ::1/128 is the loopback address.

q: A DHCP starvation attack works by doing what?
options: Speeding up the assignment of DHCP addresses
Blocking DNS replies to client requests
Exhausting the address pool with fake DHCP requests
Encrypting DHCP traffic so servers cannot read it
explain: The attacker floods the server with requests using fake MAC addresses until the pool is empty, denying addresses to real clients and possibly enabling a rogue DHCP server. DHCP snooping with rate limiting helps mitigate it.

q: BGP Flowspec is used to do what?
options: Replace all interior routing protocols
Distribute traffic-filtering and DDoS mitigation rules through BGP
Encrypt sessions between BGP peers
Assign IP addresses to BGP peers
explain: Flowspec extends BGP to push flow-based filter rules, such as drop or rate-limit actions, to routers quickly. This lets DDoS mitigation rules spread upstream fast during an attack.

q: Goodput is best defined as which of the following?
options: The total bandwidth of a link
The latency experienced by packets
The raw throughput including all protocol overhead
Useful application payload delivered, excluding overhead
explain: Goodput measures only the useful application data that actually gets delivered, excluding headers and retransmissions. It is always lower than the raw throughput of the same link.

q: A user enters the wrong WPA passphrase. What is the most likely result?
options: A faster association to the access point
A successful connection without an IP address
The SSID disappearing from the network scan
Repeated authentication failures
explain: An incorrect passphrase fails the WPA authentication handshake, so the client retries and keeps failing rather than connecting. Verify the passphrase, watching for special-character entry mistakes.

q: The DSCP value EF (Expedited Forwarding) is intended primarily for which traffic?
options: Best-effort data traffic
Streaming video traffic
Bulk file transfer traffic
Voice traffic requiring expedited forwarding
explain: EF (DSCP 46) marks low-latency traffic such as voice and receives priority queuing. Assured Forwarding (AF) classes handle other traffic types in tiers below EF.

q: A network-attached storage (NAS) appliance provides which service?
options: Block-level storage over a direct cable only
File-level shared storage over the network
Tape backup services only
Storage that cannot be shared with clients
explain: NAS shares files over the LAN using protocols such as SMB or NFS, so multiple clients access the same file storage. Block-level storage describes SAN, not NAS.

q: An application fails when passing through NAT. Which NAT-related items should be checked?
options: Whether NAT is translating addresses in the correct direction
Application layer gateways (ALGs) and NAT session timeout values
Whether DNS queries use TCP only
Whether all inbound ports have been opened
explain: Some protocols embed address information that needs an ALG to be rewritten correctly, and overly aggressive NAT timeouts can kill idle sessions. Checking ALGs and timeouts is the standard first step for NAT-related application failures.

q: Which protocol uses TCP port 80 by default?
options: File Transfer Protocol (FTP)
Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS)
Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)
Secure Shell (SSH)
explain: Port 80 is the well-known port for HTTP web traffic. HTTPS uses port 443, SSH uses port 22, and FTP uses ports 21 and 20.

q: A cable run fails a propagation delay test during certification. What does this result most likely indicate?
options: The cable is terminated using the wrong pinout standard
The cable has a damaged conductor causing high resistance
The cable run exceeds the maximum permitted length
The cable is receiving crosstalk from adjacent pairs
explain: Propagation delay is the time a signal takes to travel the length of the cable, so a delay failure points to a run that is too long for the standard's timing limits. Wiremap, resistance, and crosstalk failures are reported by separate tests.

q: Why should an organization actively manage the certificate lifecycle, including issuance, renewal, and revocation?
options: To restrict certificate use to web servers only
To track expiry and renewal so services do not suffer certificate-related outages
To replace TLS encryption with a simpler security protocol
To allow expired certificates to remain trusted indefinitely
explain: Tracking issuance, renewal, and revocation prevents outages caused by unexpected certificate expiry and ensures compromised certificates are removed. Automation such as ACME helps renew certificates before they expire.

q: A switch port is placed in the err-disabled state after UDLD runs on a fiber uplink. What condition did UDLD detect?
options: A bidirectional link operating at the wrong speed
A spanning-tree BPDU arriving on an access port
Light traveling in only one direction on the fiber link
A duplicate IP address on devices using the link
explain: UDLD monitors a link to confirm traffic flows in both directions. A unidirectional fiber link, often from a faulty strand or transceiver, is shut down to prevent spanning-tree and forwarding problems.

q: A technician brings a known-good laptop to a desk where a user's computer cannot connect to the network. What is the purpose of the laptop?
options: To replace the user's computer permanently
To serve as a trusted test endpoint for isolating the fault
To bypass the access switch for all desk users
To provide the user with temporary email access
explain: Testing the same wall jack and cable with known-good hardware separates a client problem from a cabling or switch problem. If the laptop works, the fault is in the original computer; if it also fails, the fault is in the path.

q: How long is an IPv6 address, and how is it normally written?
options: 32 bits, written as four decimal octets
128 bits, written as eight hexadecimal groups
48 bits, written as six hexadecimal octets
64 bits, written as four hexadecimal groups
explain: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses written as eight 16-bit hexadecimal groups, also called hextets. IPv4 uses 32 bits, and a MAC address uses 48 bits.

q: What does Single Root I/O Virtualization (SR-IOV) allow a virtual machine to do?
options: Share the host server's CPU scheduler with other guests
Use a fully software-emulated network adapter in the hypervisor
Access physical NIC hardware directly through virtual functions
Connect to the network without any physical NIC installed
explain: SR-IOV lets a physical NIC present multiple virtual functions that VMs can use directly. This bypasses much of the hypervisor's virtual switch, reducing overhead to near-native levels.

q: Why is post-change verification performed after a network change is implemented?
options: To document that a change was originally requested
To approve the change before any work begins
To confirm that services work as intended after the change
To schedule the next routine maintenance window
explain: Post-change verification confirms the change achieved its goal and did not break related services. The ticket should only be closed after this health check passes.

q: What is jitter on a network link?
options: The total bandwidth available on the link
The variation in delay between arriving packets
The percentage of packets lost during transmission
The maximum throughput the link can sustain
explain: Jitter is the variation in packet latency, not the average latency itself. High jitter disrupts voice and video, so QoS is used to give that traffic steady, prioritized delivery.

q: What is the purpose of service-level agreement (SLA) reporting?
options: To record informal estimates of network performance
To compare pricing between competing service vendors
To schedule routine maintenance for network devices
To compare actual performance against agreed service commitments
explain: SLA reports measure results such as uptime and response time against the commitments in the agreement. They create accountability and show whether the provider met its obligations.

q: Which service uses TCP port 21 for control connections and TCP port 20 for active-mode data transfer?
options: Secure Shell, for remote administration
Telnet, for unencrypted terminal access
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, for sending email
File Transfer Protocol, for transferring files
explain: FTP uses port 21 for the control channel and port 20 for data in active mode. SSH uses port 22, Telnet uses port 23, and SMTP uses port 25.

q: At which layer of the OSI model does TCP operate?
options: Layer 3, the Network layer
Layer 7, the Application layer
Layer 4, the Transport layer
Layer 2, the Data Link layer
explain: TCP is a Transport layer (Layer 4) protocol that provides reliable, ordered end-to-end delivery. UDP operates at the same layer without TCP's reliability mechanisms.

q: What is a key characteristic of a Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) tunnel?
options: It provides strong encryption for tunneled traffic by default
It can carry only IPv4 unicast traffic between endpoints
It can encapsulate many protocols but provides no encryption by itself
It requires a TLS certificate on each tunnel endpoint
explain: GRE encapsulates a wide range of protocols, including multicast and routing-protocol traffic, inside an IP tunnel. Because GRE alone does not encrypt, it is commonly paired with IPsec when confidentiality is required.

q: A vendor publishes a security advisory (PSIRT) affecting network devices currently in use. What should the network team do?
options: Forward the advisory to the vendor's sales team for a hardware quote
Wait until the next annual hardware refresh to review it
Promptly assess exposure and apply a patch or mitigation as needed
Disable every affected device until the vendor releases new hardware
explain: Vendor security advisories are vulnerability intelligence for products you own. The team should triage them promptly, determine which devices are exposed, and patch or mitigate according to risk.

q: What distinguishes a SYN scan, also called a half-open scan, from a full TCP connect scan?
options: It sends a SYN packet and completes the full three-way handshake
It sends UDP datagrams instead of TCP packets to each port
It connects to the port and then transfers a test file
It sends a SYN packet and ends the connection before the handshake completes
explain: In a SYN scan the scanner replies to a SYN-ACK with a reset instead of the final ACK, so the handshake never completes. This reveals whether the port is open while creating less application-level logging than a full connection.

q: What is the protocol data unit (PDU) at the Transport layer (Layer 4) called?
options: A frame, as used at the Data Link layer
A bit, as used at the Physical layer
A segment for TCP or a datagram for UDP
A packet, as used at the Network layer
explain: At Layer 4 the PDU is a segment for TCP and a datagram for UDP. Layer 3 uses packets, Layer 2 uses frames, and Layer 1 transmits bits.

q: Which organization created the OSI reference model?
options: Cisco Systems, as a proprietary networking model
The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)
The International Organization for Standardization (ISO)
The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)
explain: The ISO published the OSI reference model in 1984 as a vendor-neutral framework for networking. The IETF develops Internet standards such as RFCs, and the IEEE develops standards such as 802.3 and 802.11.

q: What is the role of sequence numbers in a TCP connection?
options: They order transmitted bytes and help the receiver detect missing data
They select the route each packet takes through the network
They identify the destination application port on the receiver
They encrypt the payload so intermediate devices cannot read it
explain: TCP assigns a sequence number to transmitted bytes so the receiver can reassemble them in order and request retransmission of missing data. Acknowledgment numbers confirm what has been received.

q: A stateful firewall drops return traffic because the traffic returns through a different firewall than it left through. What is the best way to resolve this?
options: Restore path symmetry or configure an appropriate state bypass for the affected flows
Increase the bandwidth of both firewall interfaces so traffic queues clear faster
Disable NAT on every interface of both firewalls so sessions are not translated
Move all protected servers onto the same subnet as both of the firewalls
explain: Stateful firewalls track each connection, so return traffic arriving at a device that never saw the original packets looks out of state and is dropped. Restoring a symmetric path, or carefully tuning a bypass for known flows, corrects the mismatch.

q: What does a full-duplex Ethernet link allow a device to do?
options: Send and receive data only in alternating turns
Send and receive data simultaneously on the same link
Share one collision domain with several devices through a hub
Send data at twice the rated speed in one direction only
explain: Full-duplex operation uses separate transmit and receive paths, so a device can send and receive at the same time. Half-duplex operation must alternate directions and is subject to collisions.

q: How does rate limiting help protect a network service from flooding attacks?
options: It caps how many requests or packets a source can send in a given period
It blocks every packet arriving from external networks
It encrypts traffic so an attacker cannot read its contents
It assigns QoS markings that prioritize traffic by class
explain: Rate limiting sets thresholds, for example on SYN, ICMP, or DNS requests per source, and drops traffic above the threshold. This blunts floods while still allowing traffic below the limit, unlike blocking all traffic.

q: How does a host decide whether a destination IP address is on its local subnet or on a remote network?
options: By asking a DNS server to resolve the destination name
By applying its subnet mask to the destination address and comparing the resulting network
By sending the packet to the default gateway and waiting for an error
By looking up the destination MAC address in its ARP cache
explain: The host ANDs the destination address with its own subnet mask and compares the result with its own network address. A match means the destination is local and can be ARPed directly; otherwise the packet is sent to the default gateway.

q: What defines a fixed-configuration switch?
options: It has a predetermined set of ports that cannot be expanded with modules
It is designed only for use in the core layer of a campus
It accepts interchangeable line cards to change its port count
It requires a separate chassis and supervisor module to operate
explain: A fixed-configuration switch is built with a set number and type of ports. Modular switches, by contrast, accept line cards so their port count and media types can be changed.

q: A company has accumulated many overlapping monitoring tools, leaving gaps and inconsistent data between teams. What is the best response to this tool sprawl?
options: Add another monitoring tool for each team that reports a gap
Consolidate the tools into a coherent monitoring stack
Turn off alerting until the tool inventory is reviewed
Monitor only core devices and stop monitoring access devices
explain: Too many overlapping tools create blind spots, duplicate alerts, and inconsistent data. Consolidating to a rationalized stack gives complete, consistent visibility.

q: A backup WAN link has a monthly data cap. How should failover to that link be planned?
options: Route all production traffic over the backup link at all times
Fail over only user workstations and leave servers on the failed link
Use traffic shaping and policies to limit non-critical traffic during failover
Disable the backup link whenever utilization begins to rise
explain: Backup links often have caps or overage charges, so failover plans should prioritize critical traffic and shape or block non-essential traffic. This keeps essential services running without exhausting the cap.

q: What does a web application firewall (WAF) primarily protect?
options: Email servers, by filtering spam and phishing messages before delivery
Stored database records, by auditing the queries made against the data
Network segments, by controlling Layer 3 access between subnets
Web applications from Layer 7 attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting
explain: A WAF inspects HTTP and HTTPS traffic at Layer 7 and blocks web attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. It protects the web application itself rather than acting as a general network firewall.

q: How is a failing optical network terminal (ONT) on a fiber service typically diagnosed?
options: By testing the DSL sync rate on the customer's line
By replacing the customer's router before any testing
By checking the customer's account for billing restrictions
By checking optical receive power levels and swapping the ONT if it is faulty
explain: The ONT terminates the provider's fiber at the customer site. Checking the optical receive level shows whether light is reaching the device within specification, and the provider replaces an ONT that has failed.

q: What do IPv6 privacy extensions provide for a client device?
options: A permanent address derived directly from the device's MAC address
Temporary, randomized interface addresses that change over time
A translation service that converts IPv6 traffic to IPv4
Encryption for the headers of all IPv6 packets
explain: Privacy extensions generate temporary, randomized interface identifiers instead of a stable address derived from the MAC address. Because these addresses rotate, outside observers cannot easily track a device across networks.

q: How is a CI/CD pipeline applied to network configuration changes?
options: Changes are applied directly to production devices without prior testing
Configuration backups are taken only after a deployment finishes
Documentation is updated manually several months after each deployment
Configurations are tested in the pipeline before they are deployed
explain: A network CI/CD pipeline typically lints a configuration, tests it in a lab, deploys it to a small canary group, and only then rolls it out to production. Testing before deployment catches errors while their impact is still contained.

q: What does a repeater do on a network segment?
options: It filters forwarded frames by destination MAC address
It regenerates the incoming signal to extend the segment distance
It routes packets between different IP networks
It assigns IP addresses to devices joining the segment
explain: A repeater is a Layer 1 device that regenerates and retimes the signal so it can travel farther. It does not read frames or make forwarding decisions, which distinguishes it from a switch or a router.

q: How does Differentiated Services (DiffServ) mark a packet for QoS treatment?
options: With the VLAN ID carried in the 802.1Q tag
With the source MAC address carried in the frame
With the Time to Live value in the IP header
With the DSCP value carried in the IP header
explain: DiffServ uses the Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP), a 6-bit field in the IP header, to classify a packet. Each router then applies the per-hop behavior associated with that marking.

q: A firewall's state table is completely full and new connections are being dropped. What does this indicate?
options: A DNS failure is preventing name resolution for new flows and must be corrected first
New connections are being dropped by an upstream ISP rate limiter
Session state is exhausted, possibly by a flood, so the source should be investigated and timeouts tuned
The routing table has run out of entries for new subnets and must be summarized
explain: The state table tracks every active connection, and when it fills, the firewall has nowhere to record new sessions and drops them. This can result from a SYN flood or overly long timeouts, so the traffic source and timeout settings should be checked.

q: A host has the address 192.168.1.100 with a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0. What network address is produced by ANDing the host address with the mask?
explain: Bitwise ANDing of 192.168.1.100 with 255.255.255.0 keeps the first three octets and zeroes the host octet, giving the network address 192.168.1.0. Hosts on this /24 network share that network portion.

q: A wireless client reports a received signal strength indicator (RSSI) of -85 dBm. What experience should be expected for that client?
options: Excellent throughput with a strong, clean signal
Faster roaming between access points than other clients
Poor connectivity with frequent retries and possible drops
A strong signal indicating the client is close to an access point
explain: An RSSI of -85 dBm is close to the typical noise floor, so the client will use low data rates, retry often, and may disconnect. Values around -67 dBm or stronger are generally needed for reliable voice-grade service.

q: How should threat intelligence feeds be used in network defense?
options: To inform blocking of known malicious addresses and support threat hunting
To replace the perimeter firewall as the primary control
To generate new passwords for administrative accounts
To provide DNS resolution for internal client devices
explain: Threat intelligence feeds supply indicators of compromise such as known-bad IP addresses and domains, which firewalls and DNS filters can block automatically. They complement, rather than replace, the firewall and support investigations by security analysts.

q: What does a compliance audit of network devices verify?
options: That device configurations match the organization's policy
That the network consistently achieves its maximum throughput
That users have memorized the organization's password policy
That every device runs the newest available feature release
explain: Compliance auditing compares running configurations against an approved policy baseline, checking items such as password settings, SNMP configuration, and hardening controls. Deviations are reported so they can be corrected.

q: What is a full mesh topology?
options: Each node connects only to a single central switch
Nodes are connected in a single continuous ring
Nodes are connected in a line from one end to the other
Every node has a direct connection to every other node
explain: In a full mesh, every node connects directly to every other node, which provides maximum redundancy. The cost is the number of links required, n(n-1)/2, which grows quickly as nodes are added.

q: What is crosstalk in a copper cable?
options: Interference coupled between adjacent wire pairs
Loss of signal strength as a signal travels over distance
A reflection caused by an impedance mismatch in the cable
A difference in arrival time between the fastest and slowest pairs
explain: Crosstalk is unwanted signal coupling from one pair onto a neighboring pair. Twisting the pairs at different rates reduces this interference, and damaged or poorly terminated cable allows more of it.

q: What is the main role of a virtual firewall in a virtualized environment?
options: To provide physical port security for hypervisor hosts
To assign virtual IP addresses to newly created guests
To create scheduled backups of virtual machine images
To inspect and segment traffic flowing between virtual machines
explain: Traffic between VMs on the same host may never reach a physical firewall, so a virtual firewall inspects that east-west traffic inside the virtual environment. This allows segmentation and policy enforcement between virtual workloads.

q: Why are written shift handoff notes important for a network operations team?
options: They record only projects that have already been completed
They allow managers to skip reviewing open incidents
They transfer context about open issues from one shift to the next
They replace formal incident tickets for all outages
explain: Handoff notes carry the current status, recent actions, and pending items for open issues to the incoming shift. Without them, problems can be dropped or work duplicated overnight.

q: Users repeatedly loop back to a captive portal login page after signing in. What should be checked to fix the problem?
options: Replacing every access point in the affected area with a newer hardware model
Disabling DNS resolution on the client devices so they connect by address only
Increasing the transmit power of nearby access points to improve signal strength
Portal reachability, DNS resolution, and certificate trust before authentication
explain: Before authentication, clients must be able to resolve names and reach the portal over HTTP, and the portal certificate must be trusted. If DNS or the certificate fails validation, the client is redirected in a loop instead of completing sign-in.

q: A TCP receiver sends three duplicate acknowledgments for the same segment. What does the sender do in response?
options: It waits for the retransmission timer to expire before acting
It uses fast retransmit to resend the segment that appears to be lost
It terminates the connection and opens a new one
It increases its sending window to the maximum value
explain: Three duplicate ACKs signal that later segments arrived but one segment is missing, so TCP fast retransmit resends it without waiting for the retransmission timeout. This is a common sign of packet loss on the path.

q: Why are environmental controls important in a network equipment room?
options: They protect equipment from heat, water, and fire damage
They improve the routing performance of installed devices
They authenticate users before they enter the room
They provide backup power to equipment during an outage
explain: Environmental controls and monitoring, including HVAC, leak detection, and fire suppression, protect equipment from physical damage. A cooling failure or water leak can take down an entire room of otherwise healthy devices.

q: How does traceroute identify the routers along the path to a destination?
options: By sending one oversized packet and measuring its return time
By querying DNS for the name of each router in order
By reading the routing table stored on the source host
By sending probes with increasing TTL values and recording the time-exceeded replies
explain: Traceroute sends probes with a TTL of 1, then 2, and so on; each router that discards an expired probe returns an ICMP time-exceeded message. Collecting those replies reveals each hop in order.

q: Users across an entire site report high latency to many different destinations. Where should troubleshooting begin?
options: With the network adapter of a single affected user
With the local DNS cache on one user's computer
With the wireless settings on one user's laptop
With the provider circuit and the site's core network links
explain: A symptom affecting all users and many destinations points to shared infrastructure rather than individual endpoints. Checking the provider circuit and core links first follows the scope of the problem.

q: What is a golden configuration for a network device?
options: The approved baseline template that device configurations should match
The oldest configuration stored in the device archive
A temporary configuration used only during troubleshooting
A configuration automatically generated by the device each day
explain: A golden configuration is the approved standard build for a device type. Comparing running configurations against it reveals unauthorized changes and configuration drift.

q: What is a partial mesh topology?
options: Every node is connected directly to every other node
All nodes connect through a single central hub device
Nodes connect to each other using wireless links only
Only selected critical nodes have redundant connections to each other
explain: A partial mesh gives redundant direct links only where they matter most, typically between critical sites. It balances the resilience of a full mesh against a much lower link cost, which suits WAN backbones.

q: What is the network address of the subnet 192.168.5.0/24?
explain: For 192.168.5.0/24, the network address is 192.168.5.0, which identifies the subnet itself and cannot be assigned to a host. The address 192.168.5.255 is the directed broadcast, and 192.168.5.1 is a usable host address.

q: What does the IEEE 802.11 family of standards define?
options: Wireless local area network technologies
Structured cabling categories and installation practices
Ethernet local area networks using wired media
Broadband wide area network access technologies
explain: IEEE 802.11 defines the physical and MAC layers for wireless LANs, marketed as Wi-Fi. Wired Ethernet LANs are defined by IEEE 802.3.

q: Why do network operations teams use on-call rotations?
options: To distribute after-hours coverage fairly among team members
To ensure the same engineer handles every after-hours incident
To remove the need for any escalation procedures
To give each engineer a turn testing the monitoring tools
explain: Rotations spread after-hours work across the team on a predictable schedule, such as weekly or follow-the-sun. Clear handoffs between rotations keep incidents from being missed.

q: Voice calls on a network are choppy and robotic. What should the engineer investigate first?
options: Delays in DNS lookups performed by the phones before each call is established
Incorrect extension numbers assigned to users in the call manager database
Jitter and packet loss from congestion, including QoS treatment of voice traffic
A failing DHCP server that assigns IP addresses to phones in the voice VLAN
explain: Voice is highly sensitive to jitter and packet loss, which are usually caused by congestion or voice traffic not receiving priority treatment. Checking QoS classification, such as Expedited Forwarding, and congestion on the path is the first step.

q: Why are object groups used when building firewall access control lists?
options: They group routing neighbors so policies can be applied by peer
They compress permitted traffic to improve firewall throughput
They assign DHCP scopes to groups of internal hosts
They define named sets of hosts, networks, or ports that rules can reference
explain: An object group defines a set of hosts, networks, or services once, and many ACL entries can then reference that name. This keeps policies shorter, more consistent, and easier to audit.

q: A cable tester reports a shield continuity failure on a shielded cabling run. What does this result mean?
options: The shield is not continuous end to end, so its grounding and noise protection are broken
Two conductors in the cable are shorted together somewhere along the run
One conductor in a pair is broken along the run, creating an open circuit
The cable is terminated using the wrong T568 pinout standard at one end
explain: A shielded system only drains induced noise to ground if the shield is continuous through every connector and patch point. A continuity failure means that path is broken, and the connectors or terminations should be repaired.

q: What is the purpose of a DNS NOTIFY message?
options: To transfer an entire zone file manually between servers
To update the cache of a recursive resolver with new records
To notify client devices that a host's address has changed
To alert secondary servers that a zone has changed so they can start a transfer
explain: When a primary server's zone changes, it sends NOTIFY to its secondaries. The secondaries can then check the zone serial number and start a zone transfer promptly instead of waiting for the refresh timer.

q: What does client health monitoring in a wireless LAN provide?
options: Measurements of CPU and memory usage collected from each access point only
Throughput measurements taken at the site's WAN edge link over the same period
Error and discard counts collected from the wired switch ports serving the APs
Per-device connection quality data such as signal strength, retries, and roaming history
explain: Client health monitoring tracks the connection experience of each device, including SNR, retry rates, and roaming events. This per-client view reveals wireless problems that aggregate access-point statistics can hide.

q: What does a Sender Policy Framework (SPF) record do for a domain's email?
options: It encrypts the body of messages sent from the domain during transport
It signs message headers with the domain's private key before sending
It authorizes specific mail servers to send mail for the domain, published in DNS
It scores message content and sender reputation to classify mail as spam
explain: SPF publishes a DNS TXT record listing the servers permitted to send mail for a domain, and receiving servers check the connecting server against that list. DKIM is the mechanism that signs messages, and DMARC sets the enforcement policy.

q: What makes a DNS server authoritative for a zone?
options: It forwards all queries it receives to the root servers
It holds the zone's original records and answers definitively for them
It caches answers obtained from other servers for clients
It assigns addresses to clients on the local network
explain: An authoritative server holds the source records for its zone and answers queries for those names definitively. A recursive resolver, by contrast, queries other servers on behalf of clients and caches their answers.

q: What is the role of a border leaf switch in a spine-leaf data center fabric?
options: It acts as a spine switch interconnecting all leaf switches
It is not used because fabrics connect to routers directly
It provides ordinary server connections like any other leaf
It connects the fabric to external networks and services
explain: Border leaf switches sit at the edge of the fabric and connect it to external routers, firewalls, and services. Ordinary leaves connect servers, while spines interconnect the leaves inside the fabric.

q: Which protocol uses TCP port 22 by default?
options: Secure Shell (SSH), for secure remote administration
Telnet, for unencrypted remote terminal access
File Transfer Protocol (FTP), for transferring files
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), for sending email
explain: SSH uses TCP port 22 and provides encrypted remote administration, which is why it replaced Telnet on port 23. FTP uses ports 21 and 20, and SMTP uses port 25.

q: A switch interface for a VLAN has no IP helper address configured, and the DHCP server is on a different subnet. What is the result for clients in that VLAN?
options: DNS resolution fails for the clients, but they still obtain leases normally
Clients obtain leases because their broadcast requests are routed to the server
Routing between all VLANs on the switch stops working entirely for every client
DHCP discovery broadcasts are not forwarded, so clients cannot obtain leases across subnets
explain: DHCP discovery is a broadcast, and routers do not forward broadcasts between subnets. An IP helper address on the VLAN interface relays those requests to the DHCP server as unicast so clients can receive leases.

q: A host receives an ICMP port unreachable message in response to a UDP probe. What does this message indicate?
options: The destination host is powered off and cannot be reached
The destination host could not be found on the network
The destination service is running but chose not to send a reply
The host was reached, but no service is listening on that UDP port
explain: ICMP type 3, code 3 (port unreachable) is sent when a packet reaches the host but no process is listening on the destination UDP port. UDP port scans rely on this response to identify closed ports.

q: How much power can an original Power over Ethernet (802.3af) switch port supply?
options: Up to 30 W per port
Up to 100 W per port
Up to 15.4 W per port
Up to 60 W per port
explain: IEEE 802.3af supplies up to 15.4 W per port at the switch, of which about 12.95 W is assured at the powered device. PoE+ (802.3at) raises this to 30 W, and 802.3bt provides still higher levels.

q: In IPsec, how does the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) protocol differ from Authentication Header (AH)?
options: AH provides encryption for the payload, while ESP provides authentication only
ESP provides authentication only and does not provide any confidentiality
ESP provides encryption as well as authentication, while AH provides authentication only
Both protocols provide identical security services in every configuration
explain: ESP provides confidentiality through encryption and can also provide integrity and authentication, which is why it is widely used. AH provides integrity and origin authentication only and does not encrypt the payload.

q: Which address range is used for Automatic Private IP Addressing (APIPA)?
options: 127.0.0.0/8, the loopback range
192.168.0.0/16, a private address range
169.254.0.0/16, the link-local range
10.0.0.0/8, a private address range
explain: When a host cannot reach a DHCP server, it self-assigns an APIPA address in 169.254.0.0/16. Seeing such an address is a classic sign that DHCP failed for that host.

q: What does the TCP receive window control?
options: The route a packet follows through the network
The encryption applied to the data in each segment
The amount of data a sender may transmit before receiving an acknowledgment
The number of hops a packet may cross before it is discarded
explain: The receive window tells the sender how much data the receiver can accept before an acknowledgment is required. This sliding-window flow control adapts throughput and prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slower receiver.

q: Why should network devices forward their logs to a central syslog server?
options: To store logs only on the device that generated them
To preserve log evidence off the device in case it reboots or is compromised
To reduce the need for anyone to review device logs
To fill the central server's storage instead of local storage
explain: Local log buffers are small and are lost on reboot, and an attacker who compromises a device can erase its local logs. Forwarding to a central syslog server preserves the evidence and allows events from many devices to be correlated.

q: Which functions are handled by the Presentation layer (Layer 6) of the OSI model?
options: Routing packets between different networks
Data formatting, encryption, and compression
Framing bits for transmission across a link
Establishing and ending dialogs between hosts
explain: Layer 6 translates data between the format used by the application and a format suitable for transmission, covering tasks such as character encoding, encryption, and compression. Routing is Layer 3, framing is Layer 2, and dialog control is Layer 5.

q: What problem do NAT64 and DNS64 solve when they are used together?
options: They let IPv6-only clients reach IPv4-only servers
They are an obsolete method replaced by dual-stack routing
They let IPv6 clients communicate without any DNS service
They speed up IPv6 traffic by removing translation gateways
explain: DNS64 synthesizes an IPv6 address from an IPv4-only server's A record, and NAT64 translates between the IPv6 client and the IPv4 server. Together they let IPv6-only networks keep access to IPv4-only services.

q: What does Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (DMARC) add to email authentication?
options: It aligns SPF and DKIM results with the visible sender domain and sets the handling policy
It encrypts messages as they pass between mail servers
It requires receivers to reject all mail from domains without DKIM
It signs individual message headers using a private key
explain: DMARC checks that a message's visible From domain aligns with its SPF and DKIM results and tells receivers whether to accept, quarantine, or reject failures. It also provides aggregate reports that help domain owners stop spoofing.

q: A server responds to ping, but users cannot connect to its application. Where is the fault most likely located?
options: In the physical cabling between the user and the switch
In the IP routing between the user and the server
In ARP resolution on the user's local segment
In the service port, the application itself, or a firewall rule above Layer 3
explain: A successful ping proves Layer 3 reachability, so cabling, routing, and ARP are working. The problem is at a higher layer, such as the service not listening, the wrong port being used, or a firewall blocking the application traffic.

q: In a spine-leaf data center design, which switches connect directly to servers and aggregate their traffic into the fabric?
options: Spine switches that interconnect every leaf switch
WAN routers that connect the data center to other sites
Management switches that carry only out-of-band traffic
Leaf switches that provide server access at the edge of the fabric
explain: Leaf switches are the server-facing access and aggregation point of a spine-leaf fabric, and each leaf connects up to every spine. Spines only interconnect leaves and do not connect to servers directly.

q: What is an LC connector in a fiber-optic installation?
options: A modular copper connector used on Ethernet patch cords
A bayonet connector used on coaxial cable runs
A small form-factor fiber-optic connector with a latch
A legacy connector type that is no longer manufactured
explain: The LC connector is a small form-factor fiber connector that uses a push-pull latch and is widely used for duplex fiber links. Its small size allows higher port density than the larger SC connector.

q: Why is standing water inside an outdoor conduit a problem for a copper cabling installation?
options: It improves the electrical performance of the cable pairs
It makes the cable pairs act as a single conductor
It increases the speed at which signals travel through the cable
It degrades the cable over time through corrosion and insulation damage
explain: Water that enters a conduit attacks copper conductors and insulation over time, increasing attenuation and causing intermittent faults. Outdoor runs should use gel-filled or otherwise water-blocked cable rated for wet locations.

q: Why would an administrator schedule the 'reload in' command before making a risky change to a remote device?
options: So the device reboots to its last saved configuration if the change locks the administrator out
Because the command is a dangerous operation that deletes configurations
So the device deletes its running configuration after a set time
Because the command is required before any configuration can be saved
explain: Scheduling a reload before the change creates a safety net: if the change cuts off management access, the device reboots and discards the unsaved running configuration. If the change succeeds, the administrator cancels the reload and then saves.

q: What information does a logical network diagram show?
options: Electrical power feeds and outlet locations for each rack
Physical rack layouts and the position of each device
IP addressing, VLANs, and traffic flows between systems
Cable colors used for each type of patch connection
explain: A logical diagram abstracts away the physical hardware to show how systems connect, including addressing, VLANs, and traffic flows. A physical diagram instead shows rack layouts, rooms, and actual cable paths.

q: Why are change windows used for network maintenance?
options: They guarantee that no change will ever affect production traffic
They exist so vendors can schedule firmware releases
They are scheduled mainly for the convenience of end users
They schedule risky changes during approved, low-impact periods such as off-hours
explain: A change window reserves an approved period, usually outside peak hours, when the impact of a problem will be smallest and support staff are available. This limits the blast radius if a change goes wrong.

q: What problem does the Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) prevent in a switched network that has redundant links?
options: Collisions between devices sharing a half-duplex segment
Routing loops between different autonomous systems
Broadcast storms caused by an excessive number of hosts
Switching loops that cause broadcast storms and MAC table instability
explain: Without STP, redundant switch links create loops in which broadcast frames circulate forever and MAC tables become unstable. STP blocks selected redundant links to leave a loop-free topology, and RSTP converges faster when a link fails.

q: Why should fan and power supply status be monitored on network devices with redundant components?
options: To measure the throughput contribution of each redundant component in the device
To plan firmware upgrades for the fans and power supplies installed in the device
Because a failed redundant component can otherwise go unnoticed until a second failure causes an outage
To track which users were logged in when a hardware component failed overnight
explain: A device keeps running after one fan or power supply fails, so the failure is silent without monitoring. Alerting on component status lets staff replace the failed part before the remaining component fails and takes the device down.

q: What does BPDU Guard do when it is enabled on a switch access port?
options: It allows the port to form a trunk when a switch is connected
It is intended mainly for use on trunk ports between switches
It disables the port if a BPDU is received on it
It slows spanning-tree convergence to protect edge devices
explain: Access ports should connect only to end devices, which never send BPDUs. BPDU Guard err-disables such a port if a BPDU arrives, stopping a rogue or misconnected switch from altering the spanning-tree topology.

q: Why should debug commands be used sparingly on a production network device?
options: They are required to run continuously to keep logging enabled
They produce detailed output that can be understood only by the vendor's developers
They are powerful but can consume significant CPU, so they must be limited in scope and duration
They permanently alter the device's running configuration as soon as they are used
explain: Debug output is generated in the device's CPU path and a broad debug can overwhelm a production device. Best practice is to scope debugs with an access list, run them briefly, and turn them off immediately afterward.

q: Which capabilities did IEEE 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4) introduce to wireless LANs?
options: MIMO with multiple spatial streams and 40 MHz channels
Operation in the 6 GHz frequency band
Mandatory use of WPA3 security for all networks
Orthogonal frequency-division multiple access (OFDMA)
explain: 802.11n introduced MIMO multiple spatial streams and channel bonding to 40 MHz, raising maximum rates to 600 Mbps. The 6 GHz band arrived with Wi-Fi 6E, and OFDMA arrived with 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6).

q: How is Occam's razor applied when troubleshooting a network problem?
options: It directs the technician to assume the most complex cause first
It favors checking the simplest, most likely explanation before exotic causes
It requires documenting every possible cause before testing any of them
It requires replacing all suspect components at the same time
explain: Occam's razor prefers the explanation that requires the fewest assumptions. In practice that means checking simple causes such as a cable, power, or a recent change before suspecting a routing-protocol fault.

q: What is TCP windowing?
options: It allows a sender to transmit multiple segments before waiting for an acknowledgment
It is the mechanism TCP uses to route segments to the receiver
It requires the window size to remain fixed at a single segment
It is the method TCP uses to encrypt segments in transit
explain: Windowing lets a sender keep multiple unacknowledged segments in flight up to the advertised window size. Larger windows improve throughput, especially on high-bandwidth, high-latency paths, compared with sending one segment at a time.

q: What do health checks on a load balancer accomplish?
options: They verify that client connections are using strong encryption
They are used only to collect statistics for client reporting
They detect failed servers and remove them from the load balancing pool
They assign IP addresses to servers when they join a pool
explain: Health checks probe backend servers at Layer 4 or Layer 7 and stop sending them traffic when they fail a probe. Traffic returns automatically once a server passes its checks again.

q: What does a cable certifier do for a new copper installation?
options: It performs only a basic continuity check of each conductor
It estimates cable performance without measuring the installation
It validates the installation against the specified category performance standard
It is used mainly to locate cables hidden behind walls
explain: A certifier measures length, wiremap, attenuation, crosstalk, and other parameters and compares them with the limits for the cable's category, producing a documented pass or fail. Passing certification is usually required for the manufacturer's installation warranty.

q: A cable test result indicates a short in a copper run. What fault does this describe?
options: One conductor is broken, leaving an open circuit
The pair is terminated into the wrong pins at the patch panel
Electromagnetic interference is being coupled into the pair
Two conductors are touching each other where they should be isolated
explain: A short means two conductors are in electrical contact when they should be separate, often because of a damaged jacket or a poor punch-down. An open is the opposite fault, where a conductor is broken.

q: An IP phone boots successfully but is placed on the data VLAN instead of the voice VLAN. What should be checked?
options: Whether the phone's mailbox has been configured correctly
Whether DNS records exist for the phone's hostname
Whether the WAN circuit has enough bandwidth for voice
LLDP-MED or CDP discovery and the switchport voice VLAN configuration
explain: Phones typically learn their voice VLAN from the switch through CDP or LLDP-MED, based on the switchport voice VLAN setting. If that configuration or discovery is missing or mismatched, the phone stays on the data VLAN.

q: Wireless users experience dropped connections while moving between coverage areas. What is the most likely cause?
options: Access points are providing too much overlapping coverage
Clients are roaming too quickly between access points
Poor cell overlap or poorly tuned roaming thresholds
A DNS problem that appears only while clients are moving
explain: Roaming needs roughly 15-20 percent cell overlap so a client can find the next access point before losing the current one. Gaps in coverage or thresholds that make clients cling to, or leave, an access point at the wrong time cause drops during movement.

q: What does switch port security control on an access port?
options: The number of VLANs that may be carried on the port
The number of MAC addresses that may be learned on the port
The amount of bandwidth the attached device may use
The speed at which the attached device must negotiate
explain: Port security limits how many source MAC addresses a port may learn and can use sticky learning to remember legitimate devices. A violation can shut the port down or restrict traffic, which helps block unauthorized devices.

q: Why is the TCP maximum segment size (MSS) adjusted on VPN tunnel interfaces?
options: To increase segment size so fewer packets are needed on the LAN
To account for encapsulation overhead so segments are not fragmented or black-holed
Because the adjustment is required only on local area network interfaces
To change the encryption algorithm negotiated by the tunnel
explain: Tunnel encapsulation adds header bytes, so a full-size segment may exceed the tunnel MTU and be fragmented or silently dropped when fragmentation is blocked. Clamping the MSS, often to about 1360 bytes, sizes TCP segments to fit the tunnel.

q: Wi-Fi is slow for every client connected to the same access point. What is the most likely area to investigate?
options: Whether the site's internet connection is working correctly
The access point itself, its wired backhaul, or interference on its channel
A device driver problem affecting one particular client
A DNS problem affecting name resolution for all websites
explain: When all clients of one access point are affected, the shared infrastructure is the suspect: channel utilization and interference, the access point's health, or its wired backhaul link. A single-client cause would not affect every user of that access point.

q: Why should a host suspected of being compromised be quarantined promptly?
options: Because the host's user must approve isolation before it can begin
Because investigation is faster if the host keeps full network access
Because quarantined hosts lose all forensic evidence immediately
To isolate the host from the network and stop the potential spread of the compromise
explain: Quarantining a suspect host contains the incident by cutting off paths to other systems and data while the host is investigated. Isolation should happen as soon as malware is credibly suspected, before detailed analysis.

q: How much power can a Power over Ethernet Plus (PoE+, 802.3at) switch port supply?
options: Up to 30 W per port
Up to 5 W per port
Up to 60 W per port
Up to 15.4 W per port
explain: IEEE 802.3at (PoE+) supplies up to 30 W per port at the switch, about double the 15.4 W of original 802.3af PoE. This supports more demanding devices such as pan-tilt-zoom cameras and multi-radio access points.

q: How does TACACS+ handle authentication, authorization, and accounting for device administration?
options: It separates authentication, authorization, and accounting into distinct functions
